modules.summary: A number trick begins with a number nobody has revealed. Naming it with a letter lets you carry it through every step, and the letter cancelling is what forces the same ending every time.

media.title: How Did She Know Your Number?
media.context: This is the chapter opener and it plays before any objective. It covers the textbook's opening set of tricks and withholds every explanation: no letter is introduced, no cancellation is shown and no pyramid or grid rule is stated. Students arrive with expressions from Class 7.
media.description: Think of a number, double it, add ten, halve it and take away the number you started with, and the answer is five for everybody in the room. A pyramid gives up its top cell before the middle rows are written, and a grid puzzle yields its largest product to somebody who never tries the arrangements.
media.teaching_notes: Learning objective: Arouse curiosity about number tricks that work for everybody, before any explanation. Key teaching points: 1) A trick can succeed without the performer knowing the number. 2) The same answer arises whatever the starting number. 3) A prediction can beat a search. 4) Writing the unknown down is the shared move. Common misconceptions: 1) Students often assume a mind reading trick relies on cues or memory. 2) Students often test a trick a few times and stop wondering why. Pause points: 0:32, at the end of nobody said a word: ask the class to run the trick with their own number. 1:17, just before the opening question: ask how the top of the pyramid could be predicted. Questions to ask: before viewing, ask whether the trick could ever fail. After viewing, ask what the three tricks might share.
media.generation_prompt:
INTENT
    Make three separate tricks work without memory or luck, and hint that writing the unknown down explains all of them.

  STORY
    A mind reading trick, a predicted pyramid and an unsearched grid all succeed for the same unstated reason.

  RENDERER
    Manim Community Edition v0.18 or later. Scene subclass.
    1920x1080, 16:9, 30 fps. Default frame is 14.22 x 8 units. All content
    inside a 4 percent safe margin. Nothing cropped.

  CHAPTER VISUAL LANGUAGE, repeat verbatim in every video of this chapter
    Background: dark slate #1F2937.
    Primary object / first set: teal #0072B2.
    Secondary object / second set: amber #E69F00.
    Shared or agreeing: green #009E73.
    Focus or highlight: reddish purple #CC79A7.
    Neutral construction lines, axes, ticks: grey #6B7280.
    Wrong, rejected or impossible case only: muted red #D55E00.
    Text off white. Body 36 px equivalent, labels 28 px.
    Prose uses Text. Mathematics uses MathTex with standard LaTeX only.
    Flat fills, uniform line weights, no gradients or glow.

  ASSETS
    No external files. No image, SVG, font or audio imports. Build everything
    from Manim primitives: Line, Arc, Circle, Polygon, Dot, Arrow, Brace,
    NumberLine, Axes, Table, VGroup.

  MATHEMATICAL TRUTH MODEL
    Every value below is the only value that may appear on screen.
    the trick: think of a number, double it, add ten, halve it, take away the number you started with
    the answer: five, for everybody in the room
    what nobody did: say their number out loud
    the pyramid: filled in from the bottom row, with the top cell predicted before the middle rows are written
    the grid puzzle: gives up its largest product to somebody who never tries all the arrangements
    the claim: these are not guesses and they are not memory
    withheld: the letter, the cancellation and every rule

  SCENE PLAN
    Total running time 90 seconds across 6 scenes.

    Scene 1. Five, for everybody
      Duration: 16 seconds.
      On screen at the start: an empty dark slate frame.
      Beats:
      at 0.2 s  Write(s1_caption) over 0.9 s, to set the frame of the scene.
      at 3.3 s  Create(s1_boxes) over 1.5 s, lag_ratio 0.35, to grow the chain from left to right.
      at 7.0 s  GrowArrow(s1_arrows) over 1.0 s, lag_ratio 0.3, to join each stage to the next.
      at 10.2 s  FadeIn(s1_flownote) over 0.8 s, to state the observation the scene has just made.
      at 13.2 s  FadeOut(s1_boxes, s1_arrows, s1_flownote) over 0.6 s, lag_ratio 0.05, to clear the frame, keeping only what carries on.
      Narration: "Think of a number. Double it, add ten, halve it, then take away the number you started with. The answer is five, and it is five for everybody in the room without exception."
      Persists into the next scene: s1_caption.

    Scene 2. Nobody said a word
      Duration: 16 seconds.
      On screen at the start: s1_caption.
      Beats:
      at 0.2 s  ReplacementTransform(s1_caption, s2_caption) over 0.9 s, to carry the caption forward rather than redrawing it.
      at 2.8 s  FadeIn(s2_sub) over 0.9 s, to state the situation.
      at 5.5 s  Indicate(s2_sub) over 0.8 s, to press on the surprising part.
      at 8.0 s  FadeIn(s2_lines) over 1.4 s, lag_ratio 0.35, to lay the observations down one under another.
      at 11.1 s  FadeIn(s2_note) over 0.8 s, to state the observation the scene has just made.
      at 13.7 s  FadeOut(s2_sub, s2_lines, s2_note) over 0.6 s, lag_ratio 0.05, to clear the frame, keeping only what carries on.
      Narration: "Nobody said their number out loud at any point, and yet every single starting number anybody chose came out at exactly the same answer, which is not at all how guessing normally behaves."
      Persists into the next scene: s2_caption.

    Scene 3. A predicted pyramid
      Duration: 16 seconds.
      On screen at the start: s2_caption.
      Beats:
      at 0.2 s  ReplacementTransform(s2_caption, s3_caption) over 0.9 s, to carry the caption forward rather than redrawing it.
      at 3.3 s  Create(s3_table) over 1.8 s, lag_ratio 0.22, to reveal the table row by row.
      at 7.2 s  FadeIn(s3_tnote) over 0.8 s, to state the observation the scene has just made.
      at 10.2 s  Indicate(s3_caption) over 0.9 s, to hold the eye on what has just appeared.
      at 13.2 s  FadeOut(s3_table, s3_tnote) over 0.6 s, lag_ratio 0.05, to clear the frame, keeping only what carries on.
      Narration: "Then a pyramid of numbers is filled in from its bottom row, and the top cell is predicted correctly before anybody has bothered to write down a single one of the middle rows."
      Persists into the next scene: s3_caption.

    Scene 4. And a grid, unsearched
      Duration: 15 seconds.
      On screen at the start: s3_caption.
      Beats:
      at 0.2 s  ReplacementTransform(s3_caption, s4_caption) over 0.9 s, to carry the caption forward rather than redrawing it.
      at 3.1 s  FadeIn(s4_chips) over 1.4 s, lag_ratio 0.18, to bring the row in one chip at a time.
      at 6.6 s  Indicate(s4_chips) over 0.9 s, lag_ratio 0.1, to sweep across the whole row.
      at 9.5 s  FadeIn(s4_note) over 0.8 s, to state the observation the scene has just made.
      at 12.4 s  FadeOut(s4_chips, s4_note) over 0.6 s, lag_ratio 0.05, to clear the frame, keeping only what carries on.
      Narration: "A grid puzzle gives up its largest product to somebody who never once tries all the possible arrangements, which means they were not searching for it at all in the first place."
      Persists into the next scene: s4_caption.

    Scene 5. Not guesses, not memory
      Duration: 14 seconds.
      On screen at the start: s4_caption.
      Beats:
      at 0.2 s  ReplacementTransform(s4_caption, s5_caption) over 0.9 s, to carry the caption forward rather than redrawing it.
      at 2.5 s  FadeIn(s5_sub) over 0.9 s, to state the situation.
      at 4.8 s  Indicate(s5_sub) over 0.8 s, to press on the surprising part.
      at 7.0 s  FadeIn(s5_lines) over 1.4 s, lag_ratio 0.35, to lay the observations down one under another.
      at 9.8 s  FadeIn(s5_note) over 0.8 s, to state the observation the scene has just made.
      at 12.0 s  FadeOut(s5_sub, s5_lines, s5_note) over 0.6 s, lag_ratio 0.05, to clear the frame, keeping only what carries on.
      Narration: "These are not guesses and they are certainly not memory. Something about writing the unknown quantity down makes the whole of each trick suddenly visible from the outside."
      Persists into the next scene: s5_caption.

    Scene 6. The opening question
      Duration: 13 seconds.
      On screen at the start: s5_caption.
      Beats:
      at 0.2 s  AddTextLetterByLetter(s6_question) over 1.8 s, to let the question land word by word.
      at 4.1 s  Create(s6_rule) over 0.6 s, to underline the question.
      at 6.8 s  FadeIn(s6_qsub) over 0.7 s, to name where the student will go looking.
      at 9.5 s  Circumscribe(s6_question) over 1.4 s, to hold the question as the closing image.
      Narration: "So what exactly is it that makes a trick visible from the inside? Three separate tricks, and one single explanation quietly sitting behind all three of them."
      Persists into the next scene: nothing, this is the last scene.

  ANIMATION RULES
    Prefer animation over narration wherever a concept can be shown.
    Every scene contains at least one transformation that carries meaning.
    No scene holds a static frame for more than 3 seconds.
    Reveal progressively; never dump a finished diagram in one Create.
    On-screen text minimal; no paragraph of prose on screen at any time.
    Objects that persist across scenes are transformed, never recreated.
    No decorative-only animation.

  MATHEMATICAL ACCURACY, highest priority
    100 percent accurate to NCERT Ganita Prakash for Class 8. Correct
    notation, terminology, symbols and labels as used in the Class 8
    textbook. Proportions true wherever proportion carries meaning; if a
    figure is not to scale it must say so on screen. No transformation may
    pass through a mathematically false intermediate state.

  LANGUAGE
    British spelling. No em dash and no en dash anywhere, in narration or on
    screen. Readable aloud by a student of this grade. Indian names and places
    for any person or setting.

  NEGATIVE CONSTRAINTS
    No value, label or claim absent from the truth model.
    No rule, formula, method or answer from any later part of the chapter.
    Nothing is taught here; the film only opens questions.
    No text outside the safe margin, no overlapping labels.
    No external assets, watermarks or branding.
    No particles, sparkles or glow.

  SELF-CHECK BEFORE OUTPUT
    1. Scene durations sum to exactly 90 seconds across 6 scenes.
    2. Every number, count and label on screen appears in the truth model and nowhere else.
    3. Every mobject named in a beat is declared in the inventory before it is used.
    4. Every persisting mobject is transformed into its next form, never recreated.
    5. No scene holds a static frame for more than 3 seconds.
    6. All geometry lies within x in [-6.8, 6.8] and y in [-3.8, 3.8]; nothing is cropped.
    7. No label overlaps another label; buff at least 0.2 everywhere.
    8. British spelling throughout, and no em dash or en dash in narration or on screen.
    9. Nothing in the film teaches a rule or reveals a later result.
    10. The film closes on curiosity about the chapter, not on an answer.

concepts.concept_name: Introduction

media.title: Letter Meaning Diagnostic
media.context: CBSE Class 8, Algebra Play, the chapter's entry beat: what a letter in an expression MEANS, fixed before any expression is built or manipulated. The content is NCERT's letter-number idea (Ganita Prakash Cl.7 Ch.4) re-established ahead of Class 8 manipulation. The class has met multiplication written without a sign and substituting a number for a letter; it has NOT met like terms, equations or any manipulation, and none is used here. The tool targets the two dominant errors on this topic: letter-as-object ('fruit-salad algebra': s means students) and letter-as-fixed-label (a letter read as a name that cannot vary), plus the unit letter read as an unknown.

finish.normal: The same panel with no star and evaluated false. There is no play again loop.
finish.practice: A full screen celebration carrying a star rating from the real score, all correct 3, 60 per cent or more 2, else 1 and never 0, plus a what you have learned panel and Review. The star screen offers Review, which walks every item showing the student's reading, the correct reading and the substitution that separates them.
whatYouLearned: A letter in algebra stands for a number, never for an object, a unit or a name
6r means six times the number of rows, which is why r has to be defined before it is used
Substituting a value is the test: only the number reading gives an answer that means anything

overview.goal: The student states that a letter stands for a number rather than for an object, rewrites a mislabelled use, and substitutes a value to show which reading survives.
overview.theme: Class 8 register: clean geometric line work, one accent plus one second accent, no decoration Setting: A plain working ground carrying one written sentence across the top and two reading cards beneath it, the way a line of a notebook is read twice over before either reading is trusted. Character: none, because this mount is an instrument. Premise: A class splits over whether the letter in 6r counts the rows or names them, and one substituted value is asked to settle it.
overview.concept: A letter in algebra stands for a number. It does not abbreviate an object, a unit or a label. Writing s for students and then using 6s as though it meant six students confuses a count with the thing counted, and the confusion shows the moment a value is substituted.
overview.purpose: The student states that a letter stands for a number rather than for an object, rewrites a mislabelled use, and substitutes a value to show which reading survives.
overview.blackboard: Any theorem, derivation, proof, formula or numerical calculation that takes MORE THAN TWO mathematical steps is written on the blackboard step by step, one step below the previous one, in logical order. Never show all the steps at once and never combine two calculations into one line. One calculation per line.
overview.uiOverview: Sentence, reading cards, substitution strip stacked. On a 390 px frame the cards stack vertically and the highlighted letter keeps a 44 px hit target. The Finish button renders ONLY in Practice and Free Play, gated positively on the mode. The HOST renders the mode selector, the language switcher and the mute in its own bar; this tool does not draw them and never lists the mode selector as a student control.
overview.neverRemove: Do not reveal the correct reading while a judgement is still open, and never quietly repair a student's rewrite before substituting into it. A repaired rewrite would remove the very failure that carries the argument.
overview.predictFirst: Step 1 of every mode that teaches opens with the CONTENT HIDDEN. The student commits a prediction before the tool shows any result, marked answer, filled table or read out. Committing emits prediction_made, which unlocks step 1 so the real result animates in BESIDE the guess.
overview.flowOfUnderstanding: Predict, then observe, then compare, then conclude. Expressions are built from operations on numbers, and operations only act on numbers. If s were the word students then 6s would be six copies of a word, which cannot be added to or compared with anything. Substituting a value is the test: under the number reading the expression produces a sensible count, and under the label reading it produces nonsense the student can see for themselves. Concept reveals the idea in 3 beats, Learn works the five checkpoints solved, Practice serves six drawn questions scored, and Free Play unlocks everything with nothing required.

scenes.animation: Judgement: the chosen card lifts and the other dims, so the commitment is visible before it is tested.
scenes.explanation: Blackboard lines, in order: A corner marked A is a name for a position, and a name cannot be doubled or added to. | In there are A apples, the letter is the count of apples. | Substituting 5 into the corner name gives the corner 5, which means nothing at all. | Substituting 5 into the count gives 5 apples, which the basket can hold. | Only the second use is algebra; the first is a label the diagram happens to carry. learnMode.summary: Learn, teacher operated. The worked items arrive in props.learnQuestions, mandatory checkpoints first. Each item loads its own usage, poses the judgement, then reveals the correct reading, the rewrite and the substitution together as one beat. Prev / Next move between items.
learnMode.checkpointPlan: ML1 (Easy, Edge Case): A letter is algebraic only when it stands for a number a value could replace. Breaks: A letter read as a fixed label such as a corner name rather than as a quantity that can vary. ML2 (Medium, Edge Case): A unit letter is fixed by the measuring system; an algebraic letter is a number waiting for a value. Breaks: Any letter written beside a number read as an unknown, so a unit is treated as a variable. ML3 (Medium, Conceptual): Substituting a value tests the reading, and zero is the value that separates a count from a name. Breaks: A letter read as an abbreviation for an object, so s means students rather than the number of students. ML4 (Hard, Conceptual): A correct definition names what the letter counts, so the value moves when the letter moves. Breaks: A rewrite that renames the object accepted as a definition of the letter. ML5 (Hard, Edge Case): A definition is judged by the quantity it names, not by the words chosen to name it. Breaks: Believing only one exact form of words can define a letter.

conceptMode.summary: Concept, agent driven, 3 teaching beats. Beat 1 shows a sentence using s and asks, with the reading HIDDEN, whether s means students or the number of students. Beat 2 puts both readings side by side and rewrites the faulty one. Beat 3 substitutes a test value into each reading and the label reading evaluates to nonsense, which is the refutation. The agent advances with next() / prev() / gotoStep and can compose a beat with setUsage, setReading, substitute and say.

conceptMode.teacherCallPlan: Call 1. Open on the sentence about six students in each row across r rows, with both reading cards hidden and the substitution strip empty, and ask the class to say out loud whether r means rows or the number of rows. Commit the class answer on the prediction pad. Targets the usage sentence and the highlighted letter r. Never raise a reading card before the prediction is committed, and never say which reading is correct at this call. Call 2. Bring both reading cards up together and rewrite the faulty one so the letter is defined as a number, letting the corrected sentence replace the old one in place. Point at the definition box and then at the number card. Targets the number card, the label card and the rewrite field. State no evaluated result at this call. Call 3. Substitute the test value into both cards in turn and let the label card produce its own nonsense beside the number card's count. Targets the substitution strip at a test value of 4, then both evaluated cards. Read every number you state from getState().truth, never from this plan.

observationsAndConclusions.why: Operations act on numbers only, so six copies of a word is not a thing any operation can be applied to
observationsAndConclusions.observe: The label card stops producing a number the moment a value is substituted into it
observationsAndConclusions.conclusion: A letter that abbreviates an object cannot survive substitution, which is the test that separates the two readings

observationsAndConclusions.why: Under that reading the letter is a quantity, and a quantity may take any value in its range without the sentence breaking
observationsAndConclusions.observe: The number card keeps returning a sensible count at every value tried, zero included
observationsAndConclusions.conclusion: A letter is not tied to one hidden number; it stands for whichever number the situation supplies

observationsAndConclusions.why: The expression was never the problem; what was missing was a statement of what the letter counts
observationsAndConclusions.observe: Rewriting the sentence changes nothing on screen except the stated meaning of the letter, and the expression begins to evaluate
observationsAndConclusions.conclusion: Naming the letter as a number is part of the algebra, not a formality that comes before it

media.description: One usage sentence stands across the top of a plain working ground with its letter typeset and boxed, and beneath it two reading cards take that same letter two different ways: one as the NUMBER of something, one as the word for the thing itself. A substitution strip between them carries a single value down into both cards in turn. The number card answers with a count. The word card answers with six copies of a word, struck through, because that is literally what six times a word comes to — the refutation is the arithmetic the student's own reading produced, never a verdict the tool hands down. A unit letter and a genuine point label are handled honestly too: the strip refuses to substitute into metres and names the reason, and a corner marked A evaluates to 'the corner 5', set aside as not algebra rather than marked wrong. Concept walks three beats — the idea, the three words 'the number of' that make a definition, then one value entering both cards. Learn works the five reviewed checkpoints with their results already on screen. Practice serves six drawn questions from a thirty-item pool on a difficulty ladder, hiding every evaluated result until the answer is in. Free Play unlocks five authored usages, the reading choice, the definition and rewrite boxes and a 0-20 value slider, with nothing scored.

scenes.valuesShown: Every readout stays live, so the invariants keep being computed while the student explores

concept.notation: In 6s, s is the number of students, not the word students. The expression 6s means six times that number.
concept.statement: A letter in algebra stands for a number. It does not abbreviate an object, a unit or a label. Writing s for students and then using 6s as though it meant six students confuses a count with the thing counted, and the confusion shows the moment a value is substituted.
prerequisites: substituting a number for a letter
misconceptions: A letter read as an abbreviation for an object, so s means students rather than the number of students.
A letter read as a fixed label such as a person's initial rather than as a quantity that can vary.
concept.why_it_is_true: Expressions are built from operations on numbers, and operations only act on numbers. If s were the word students then 6s would be six copies of a word, which cannot be added to or compared with anything. Substituting a value is the test: under the number reading the expression produces a sensible count, and under the label reading it produces nonsense the student can see for themselves.
worked_numbers: Six students in each row, r rows: the count is 6r, and at r equal to 4 that is 24 students.
Reading r as rows rather than as the number of rows gives 6 rows, which is not what the situation asks for.
Naming the letter first, r is the number of rows, makes the substitution check meaningful.

extra: A bus with s seats in each row and r rows, where each letter counts something
A shelf holding b books, where b is the number of books and not the word books
The letter m used for metres beside the letter d used for a distance measured in metres
A point named A on a diagram set beside the letter a used for a length
The price of one pen written as p rupees, then the cost of five pens
A tank holding l litres, where l is a count of litres and not the unit itself
A team of n players, with n set to zero to see whether the sentence still says anything
textbook: The number chosen at the start of a number trick, written as x before a single instruction is applied
The bottom row of a number pyramid named by letters so the top entry can be written in terms of them
The top left entry of a chosen calendar grid called x, with the other three written from it
A two digit number whose tens digit and units digit are each given their own letter
The chapter's opening claim that algebra works on unknown letter numbers and not on words

answer_key.worked: In 6r for six students per row across r rows, r is the number of rows; at r equal to 4 the expression gives 24, which is a count of students and confirms the reading.
answer_key.practice: Computed per item at runtime from the item's usage: the correct reading, the accepted rewrites and the value each reading produces under substitution.
answer_key.precision: The rewrite is parsed and evaluated as written, never repaired. Substitution uses exact rational arithmetic so the surviving reading is decided by the value, not by rounding.
answer_key.ground_truth: readingOf(usage) = 'number' or 'label'. rewriteForms(usage) = the accepted definitions of the letter. evaluate(studentExpression, value) = the exact value of what the student actually wrote.

blackboard.rule: Any theorem, derivation, proof, formula or numerical calculation that takes MORE THAN TWO mathematical steps is written on the blackboard step by step, one step below the previous one, in logical order.

modes.ai: The agent narrates while the board fills; the board never runs ahead of the narration.
modes.learn: The board is the reveal. Before reveal() it is empty; on reveal it fills line by line, then the answer lands last.
modes.normal: No board unless the student asks the tool to settle something, then the same line by line fill.
modes.practice: The board stays empty until the answer is checked, then fills line by line as the explanation.

blackboard.for_a_proof: State the claim first, then write and explain each step in sequence, then close on the conclusion.
blackboard.readability: Keep the board clean and uncrowded, at Class 8 reading level, with the same symbols the scene uses.
blackboard.applies_when: The explanation runs to more than two mathematical steps. Two steps or fewer may be written together.
blackboard.for_a_calculation: Show the complete working line by line, including every intermediate value, before the final answer is shown.
blackboard.one_step_per_line: Never show all the steps at once and never combine two calculations into one line. One calculation per line.
blackboard.source_of_the_lines: The `steps` array of the Learn checkpoint or Practice question on screen IS the blackboard, in order. Render one array entry per line. It is gated at build time: no entry carries two calculations.
blackboard.builds_progressively: The board fills line by line as the explanation is given, so the student can see how each step follows from the one above it. A line already written stays on the board.

edge_cases.case: A rewrite that is correct in meaning but worded differently
edge_cases.tool_behaviour: Accepted, since the check is that the letter is defined as a number and the expression parses, not that the wording matches.

edge_cases.case: A rewrite that still names an object
edge_cases.tool_behaviour: Substituted anyway and the resulting nonsense is shown, since the refutation must come from the student's own writing.

edge_cases.case: A usage where the letter genuinely is a label, such as point A
edge_cases.tool_behaviour: Marked as not an algebraic use at all and set aside, since the distinction being taught is between a number and a name.

edge_cases.case: A unit letter such as m for metres
edge_cases.tool_behaviour: Flagged as a unit rather than an unknown, and the tool asks for the quantity to be named separately from its unit.

edge_cases.case: A substitution value of zero
edge_cases.tool_behaviour: Allowed, and the tool notes that zero students is still a number while zero of the word students is not a meaning at all.

shared_state.note: Exactly what getState() returns and what rides every {type:'state'} emit. The teacher agent reads these field names, so they are a contract: renaming one silently breaks narration.

aiModeCalls.steps: next() / prev() / gotoStep(index) over the Concept beats; playDemo() auto runs them all
aiModeCalls.description: In Concept the agent orchestrates the demonstration from these calls. next() / prev() / gotoStep drive the 3 built in beats; the component calls let the agent branch a beat, for example substituting the exact value a child suggests and letting the label reading fail on its own.

postmessage.note: The tool emits {type:'ready', toolId} on mount and commands sent before it are DROPPED. Every windowMethod is also reachable as a command method.

agent_control.operator_note: Concept (ai) and Learn are TEACHER operated. The agent calls the step verbs and narrates; the class watches and answers out loud. No beat in these two modes may carry operate-the-control copy (no 'tap your guess', 'press Check', 'drag the marker'). steps: Under the number reading, s is the number of students, so 6s is 6 times that number.

teaching_notes: Beat 1 exists to fix ONE thing before anything else can be said: the letter is a number. The card shows the definition in its NCERT shape — 'r = the number of rows' — and the plate carries the expression 6r rather than any value, because a value has not been substituted yet. Ask the class out loud what r means before you read the card; the guess is the thing the next two beats test.

Beat 2 is the mechanism, and the mechanism is three words. Both cards are up, built from the SAME letter, and the only difference between them is that one says 'the number of rows' and the other says 'the word rows'. The definition clause writes itself under the sentence at this beat. Point at the three words; they are what makes a substitution possible at all.

Beat 3 is the refutation, and it must come from the arithmetic rather than from you. One value enters both cards. The number card gives 24 students. The word card gives six copies of the word 'rows', struck through, because six times a word is exactly that and nothing can be added to it or compared with it. Do not paraphrase the struck row into a sentence — the class has to see the nonsense their own reading produced. If someone offers a different value, call substitute() with it; at every value the number card still answers and the word card still does not.

media.instructions_for_student: A letter in algebra stands for a NUMBER, not for the thing being counted. In 6r, r is the number of rows, so 6r is six times that number — it is not six rows. media.context: This hook opens the first topic, straight after the chapter opener. Students have no explanation. The film must not introduce the letter and must not show any cancellation.
media.description: Pick any number and keep it secret. A friend tells you to add, double and follow a few more steps, then announces your answer without ever hearing your number. It works every time, on every friend, with every starting number.
media.teaching_notes: Learning objective: Recognise that a number trick works by structure rather than by information about the number. Key teaching points: 1) The performer never learns the starting number. 2) The steps are the same for everybody. 3) So the ending must be forced by the steps. 4) Writing the unknown as a letter makes that visible. Common misconceptions: 1) Students often assume the performer works out the number from clues. 2) Students often think the trick only works for small numbers. Pause points: 0:23, at the end of and it never fails: ask the class to try it with a very large number. 0:23, just before the open question: ask what the performer actually knows. Questions to ask: before viewing, ask whether the trick could fail. After viewing, ask what the friend needs to know.

topics.summary: A trick starts with a number nobody has told you. Calling it a letter lets you write every step as an expression and carry the mystery number through the whole trick.

content.text: When a trick says 'think of a number', you do not know which number was chosen. You can still work with it by calling it a letter, say n. Every instruction is then written as an expression in n. 'Add 8' becomes n plus 8. 'Multiply by 3' becomes 3n. 'Double, then add 4' becomes 2n plus 4. The letter records exactly what each step does, without ever choosing a value. As long as the letter is still there, the result is not a single number: it changes when the starting number changes. Only when you replace n by an actual number does the expression become one fixed value.

media.title: Substitution Machine
media.context: CBSE Class 8, Algebra Play, the module 'From mystery numbers to letters'. The skill is introduced in NCERT Class 7 Algebraic Expressions ('finding the value of an expression') and reused in Class 8. It sits where the chapter's instruction chains are turned into values, so a think-of-a-number chain can be checked at any number. Order of operations is taught here as BODMAS and the word is BRACKETS, never parentheses; the finished Class 8 answer is an exact improper fraction such as 11/4, never a mixed number and never 2.75.

finish.normal: The same panel with no star and evaluated false. There is no play again loop.
finish.practice: A full screen celebration carrying a star rating from the real score, all correct 3, 60 per cent or more 2, else 1 and never 0, plus a what you have learned panel and Review. The star screen offers Review, which walks every item showing the student's answer, the exact value and the trace that produced it.
whatYouLearned: Substitution replaces every copy of the letter with the same number at once
The structure of the expression sets the order of the operations, not the order the symbols are read
A squared term stays positive at a negative value while a linear term changes sign

overview.goal: The student substitutes a value into an expression, follows the operations in the order the structure requires, and explains why a negative value changes some terms and not others.
overview.theme: Class 8 register: clean geometric line work, one accent plus one second accent, no decoration Setting: A plain working ground with the expression written large across the top, a value slider beneath it and a trace of the working running down the panel, the way a calculation is set out line under line in a notebook. Character: none, because this mount is an instrument. Premise: A class is split over whether 3x squared plus 5x comes out positive or negative when x is minus 3, and the trace is asked to settle it one operation at a time.
overview.concept: Evaluating an expression means replacing the letter with a number and then applying the operations in the order the expression's structure sets, not in the order the symbols are read. In 3x squared the squaring acts on x alone, and at a negative value the result is positive while a term like 5x turns negative.
overview.purpose: The student substitutes a value into an expression, follows the operations in the order the structure requires, and explains why a negative value changes some terms and not others.
overview.blackboard: Any theorem, derivation, proof, formula or numerical calculation that takes MORE THAN TWO mathematical steps is written on the blackboard step by step, one step below the previous one, in logical order. Never show all the steps at once and never combine two calculations into one line. One calculation per line.
overview.uiOverview: Expression, slider, trace stacked. On a 390 px frame the trace scrolls within the panel and the slider keeps a 44 px thumb. The Finish button renders ONLY in Practice and Free Play, gated positively on the mode. The HOST renders the mode selector, the language switcher and the mute in its own bar; this tool does not draw them and never lists the mode selector as a student control.
overview.neverRemove: Do not show the result while a sign prediction is open, and never render the trace in reading order when the structure requires otherwise. A left to right trace would teach the very error the tool exists to remove.
overview.predictFirst: Step 1 of every mode that teaches opens with the CONTENT HIDDEN. The student commits a prediction before the tool shows any result, marked answer, filled table or read out. Committing emits prediction_made, which unlocks step 1 so the real result animates in BESIDE the guess.
overview.flowOfUnderstanding: Predict, then observe, then compare, then conclude. An expression is a tree of operations, and substitution changes only the leaves. The structure that decides which operation acts on what is fixed before any value arrives, so it cannot change when the value does. That is why a negative value flips the sign of an odd power and leaves an even power positive: the exponent acts on the letter alone, and the coefficient multiplies whatever comes out. Concept reveals the idea in 3 beats, Learn works the five checkpoints solved, Practice serves six drawn questions scored, and Free Play unlocks everything with nothing required.

learnMode.checkpointPlan: ML1 (Easy, Edge Case): A value of zero removes every term carrying the letter and leaves the constant untouched. Breaks: Believing the whole expression collapses to zero when the letter is zero. ML2 (Medium, Edge Case): An even power turns a negative value positive; a term with a single power keeps the sign. Breaks: Sign errors when a negative value is substituted, particularly into a squared term. ML3 (Medium, Conceptual): A coefficient sits outside the power unless a bracket puts it inside. Breaks: Squaring applied to the coefficient as well as the letter, so 3x squared at x equal to 2 is read as 36. ML4 (Hard, Edge Case): A fractional value is substituted exactly, because rounding an intermediate value moves the answer. Breaks: Believing a decimal approximation of a fraction can stand in for it mid calculation. ML5 (Hard, Edge Case): A bracket changes which operation acts on what, so the same symbols in the same order can be two expressions. Breaks: Operations applied left to right regardless of structure.

conceptMode.teacherCallPlan: Call 1. Open on 3x squared plus 5x with the slider already at minus 3, the trace collapsed and the result hidden, and ask the class to say out loud whether the answer will be positive or negative. Commit the class answer on the prediction pad. Targets the expression and the value slider at minus 3. Never open the trace before the prediction is committed. Call 2. Step the trace one operation at a time, naming the operation and letting the running value appear beside each line, so the squared term resolves before anything is added to it. Point at the squared term and then at the linear term. Targets the trace lines in order and the running value after each. Read every running value from getState().truth, never from this plan. Call 3. Move the value across zero to a positive value and let the terms that change sign pulse once as it passes. Targets the value slider at 2, the squared term and the linear term. Say which term changed sign and which did not, and read the two results from getState().truth.

EXACT ONLY: choose a fractional value and find an expression whose exact value has a denominator larger than 4.

observationsAndConclusions.why: Substitution replaces the leaves of the expression in a single act, since they are all the same letter
observationsAndConclusions.observe: Moving the slider makes every copy of the letter change together, not one after another
observationsAndConclusions.conclusion: Every occurrence of a letter in one expression carries the same value at the same moment

observationsAndConclusions.why: The exponent acts on the letter alone, so a negative value multiplied by itself gives a positive, while a single copy of it keeps its sign
observationsAndConclusions.observe: At a negative value the squared term stays positive while the linear term turns negative
observationsAndConclusions.conclusion: A sign rule is not a special case to memorise; it follows from how many copies of the value the term holds

observationsAndConclusions.why: The structure of the expression decides which operation acts on what, and that structure is fixed before any value arrives
observationsAndConclusions.observe: The trace never runs left to right across the written expression
observationsAndConclusions.conclusion: Reading order and operation order are different things, which is why the same symbols can be evaluated only one way

media.description: An expression is written large across the top of a plain working ground with a dashed scope box drawn round exactly what a power owns, and beneath it the same expression written again with the value substituted INSIDE BRACKETS - 3(-3) squared + 5(-3) - which is the NCERT written step and the whole fix for the lost-sign error. Every copy of the letter flashes to the value in ONE frame, so substitution is seen as a single simultaneous replacement rather than a series of swaps. Below the two lines the expression breaks into one COLUMN PER TERM, laid out as an equal partition of the board width: each column carries the term as written, the term with the value substituted, and a signed magnitude bar standing on ONE shared baseline with ONE shared unit, so the bar for 32 is exactly twice the bar for 16 and a negative term visibly hangs below the line the positive terms stand on. A combine strip under the columns writes the terms out and closes on the value. Moving the value across zero pulses only the terms whose sign actually changed, which separates the squared term from the linear one by what they DO rather than by a remembered rule, and a rival reading is drawn beside the real one as its own column - 3x squared against (3x) squared - so a student's wrong answer is shown to belong to a different expression rather than simply refused. The expression is parsed to a tree once and evaluated in exact rational arithmetic, so a fractional value gives an exact improper fraction and never a rounded decimal, and the trace never runs left to right across the written symbols because it is the post-order walk of the tree.

modes.normal: Free Play, student operated. The student types any expression, slides the value and steps the trace as often as they like. Nothing is scored and nothing is mandatory.
modes.practice: Practice, student operated. The bank from props.questions, one item at a time, each rendering its own expression. Predict the sign, give the value, or name the next operation in the trace. Scored, with a star finish and a Review phase that walks every item showing the student's value against the trace.

concept.notation: Substitution replaces every occurrence of the letter with the same value. The trace lists each operation as the expression tree requires it, innermost first.
concept.statement: Evaluating an expression means replacing the letter with a number and then applying the operations in the order the expression's structure sets, not in the order the symbols are read. In 3x squared the squaring acts on x alone, and at a negative value the result is positive while a term like 5x turns negative.
misconceptions: Operations applied left to right regardless of structure.
Squaring applied to the coefficient as well as the letter, so 3x squared at x equal to 2 is read as 36.
Sign errors when a negative value is substituted, particularly into a squared term.
concept.why_it_is_true: An expression is a tree of operations, and substitution changes only the leaves. The structure that decides which operation acts on what is fixed before any value arrives, so it cannot change when the value does. That is why a negative value flips the sign of an odd power and leaves an even power positive: the exponent acts on the letter alone, and the coefficient multiplies whatever comes out.
worked_numbers: 3x squared plus 5x at x equal to 2 is 12 plus 10, so 22.
At x equal to minus 3 it is 27 minus 15, so 12, since the square is positive and the linear term is negative.
At x equal to one half it is three quarters plus five halves, so thirteen quarters exactly.

answer_key.worked: 3x squared plus 5x at x equal to minus 3 gives 12, because the square makes 9 and then 27, while 5 times minus 3 is minus 15.
answer_key.practice: Computed per item at runtime from the parsed expression: the exact value as a fraction and the ordered trace of operations.
answer_key.precision: The expression is parsed to a tree once and evaluated with exact rational arithmetic, so fractional values give exact fractions rather than decimals.
answer_key.ground_truth: parse(expression) = the operation tree. evaluate(tree, value) = the exact rational result. trace(tree, value) = the ordered list of operations with the running value after each.

blackboard.rule: Any theorem, derivation, proof, formula or numerical calculation that takes MORE THAN TWO mathematical steps is written on the blackboard step by step, one step below the previous one, in logical order.

modes.ai: The agent narrates while the board fills; the board never runs ahead of the narration.
modes.learn: The board is the reveal. Before reveal() it is empty; on reveal it fills line by line, then the answer lands last.
modes.normal: No board unless the student asks the tool to settle something, then the same line by line fill.
modes.practice: The board stays empty until the answer is checked, then fills line by line as the explanation.

blackboard.for_a_proof: State the claim first, then write and explain each step in sequence, then close on the conclusion.
blackboard.readability: Keep the board clean and uncrowded, at Class 8 reading level, with the same symbols the scene uses.
blackboard.applies_when: The explanation runs to more than two mathematical steps. Two steps or fewer may be written together.
blackboard.for_a_calculation: Show the complete working line by line, including every intermediate value, before the final answer is shown.
blackboard.one_step_per_line: Never show all the steps at once and never combine two calculations into one line. One calculation per line.
blackboard.source_of_the_lines: The `steps` array of the Learn checkpoint or Practice question on screen IS the blackboard, in order. Render one array entry per line. It is gated at build time: no entry carries two calculations.
blackboard.builds_progressively: The board fills line by line as the explanation is given, so the student can see how each step follows from the one above it. A line already written stays on the board.

edge_cases.case: A negative value in a squared term
edge_cases.tool_behaviour: The trace shows the squaring applied to the value alone and the result is positive, with the coefficient multiplied afterwards.

edge_cases.case: A fractional value
edge_cases.tool_behaviour: Every running value is shown as an exact fraction, never a rounded decimal.

edge_cases.case: A value of zero
edge_cases.tool_behaviour: Terms containing the letter vanish and the constant remains, which the tool names rather than skipping.

edge_cases.case: An expression with brackets
edge_cases.tool_behaviour: The bracket is evaluated first in the trace, since the trace follows the tree rather than the reading order.

edge_cases.case: An expression the student types that will not parse
edge_cases.tool_behaviour: Returned with the position that failed, and no value is produced, since evaluation by string replacement is never attempted.

Read it as props.learnQuestions ?? props.additionalProps?.learnQuestions. When it is non empty those items ARE the Learn steps; the authored scene examples are only the fallback for a thin pool.
hostProps.showModeSelector: false in production for every maths tool. Honour it, defaulting to true (const showSelector = props.showModeSelector ?? true) so the selector still works in preview and review, and disappears live.
hostProps.additionalProps.exampleSeed: A 32 bit int the tool's mulberry32 PRNG consumes directly. The teacher agent builds its own copy of the example set from the SAME seed, so Math.random(), Date.now() or ignoring the seed desynchronises the narration from the screen in every single session.

value.description: The value substituted for the letter.

questions.description: Replaces the built in practice bank. Items are {kind:'evaluate', expression:string, value:number} | {kind:'predict_sign', expression:string, value:number} | {kind:'next_step', expression:string, value:number, index:number} | {kind:'choice', prompt, options[], correct, explain}.

traceIndex.description: How far the step trace has been advanced.

constraints: The expression is parsed to a tree once, so the trace order is correct by construction rather than by authoring.
Exact rational evaluation throughout; fractional values produce exact fractions.
Substitution never happens by string replacement, so a coefficient can never be caught up in an exponent.
The result stays hidden while a sign prediction is open.
The slider spans negative and fractional values, since that is where substitution errors cluster.

extra.concept_only: Concept carries no questions of its own. Its beats reveal the idea and then run one reasoning beat each, and every number the agent says is read from state.truth.

ai.shows: The expression, the value slider, the step trace, the running value, the teacher caption, and discrete step navigation (Prev / Step k of 3 / Next) with a progress bar.
steps: Predict: the value is set to minus 3 with the result HIDDEN. The class commits to positive or negative, out loud, and the teacher commits it on the pad. prediction_made unlocks the beat.
Trace: the operations are applied one at a time in structural order, with the running value shown after each.
Compare: the value moves from positive to negative and the trace shows which terms change sign and which do not.
ai.done_when: Beat 3 has been reached and both a positive and a negative value have been traced. Concept has no Finish button.
ai.driven_by: The teaching agent, through next() / prev() / gotoStep(index) and the component calls.
ai.opens_with: 3x squared plus 5x with the slider at minus 3, the trace collapsed and the result hidden, the predict pad open on 'Positive or negative?'.

learn.shows: One worked item: the expression, the value, the question, then the full trace and the exact value together.
steps: One beat per bank item, in the order the bank supplies: every mandatory checkpoint first in Easy, Medium, Hard order, then the random Learn slots.
learn.fallback: If props.learnQuestions arrives empty, fall back to the authored set: 3x squared plus 5x at 2; the same at minus 3; a fractional value; an expression with brackets; and a value of zero.
learn.done_when: The last Learn item has been revealed. No Finish button renders in Learn.
learn.driven_by: The teaching agent, through next() / prev(); the on screen Prev / Next also work for a reviewer.
learn.opens_with: The first mandatory checkpoint from props.learnQuestions, its expression already loaded.

normal.shows: The expression field, the slider, the trace, the running value, every control, no score and no question.
steps: No steps. Nothing is mandatory and nothing is scored.
normal.done_when: The student presses Finish, which emits finished once.
normal.opens_with: An editable expression with the slider free to move across negative and fractional values.
play_modes: SIGN SPLIT: find a value where one term of your expression is positive and another is negative, and say which power did it.
ZERO SWEEP: find every expression on the tray whose value at x equal to 0 is its own constant.
BRACKET SWAP: build two expressions with the same symbols in the same order that disagree at every value except one.
EXACT ONLY: choose a fractional value and find an expression whose exact value has a denominator larger than 4.
normal.parameter_freedom: Every adjustable parameter is unlocked inside its invariant limits, nothing is scored, nothing progresses, and no question is posed. The student sets the values, and may pose their own question and let the tool settle it, because the tool keeps computing and showing its invariants the whole time. The hunts below are starting points, not a syllabus.

practice.shows: The item's own expression, the question, the answer affordance, a running score, and the Finish button.
steps: One item at a time from props.questions; the tool never re-orders or filters the bank.
practice.review: The star screen offers Review, which walks every item showing the student's answer, the exact value and the trace that produced it.
practice.done_when: The bank is exhausted (emit bank_done, not terminal) or the student presses Finish (emit finished, once).
practice.opens_with: Item 1 of the bank, expression shown, result hidden, score at 0.

interactions.response: The substituted value and the whole trace update together.

shared_state.note: Exactly what getState() returns and what rides every {type:'state'} emit. The teacher agent reads these field names, so they are a contract: renaming one silently breaks narration.

aiModeCalls.steps: next() / prev() / gotoStep(index) over the Concept beats; playDemo() auto runs them all
aiModeCalls.description: In Concept the agent orchestrates the demonstration from these calls. next() / prev() / gotoStep drive the 3 built in beats; the component calls let the agent branch a beat, for example setting the exact value a child names and stepping the trace to the operation they doubted.

postmessage.note: The tool emits {type:'ready', toolId} on mount and commands sent before it are DROPPED. Every windowMethod is also reachable as a command method.

agent_control.operator_note: Concept (ai) and Learn are TEACHER operated. The agent calls the step verbs and narrates; the class watches and answers out loud. No beat in these two modes may carry operate-the-control copy (no 'tap your guess', 'press Check', 'drag the marker'). Keep the thinking half of the sentence ('Predict first', 'Say your answer out loud first') and drop the device half. Practice and Free Play are student operated and address the student directly.

predict_first.rule: Step 1 of every mode that teaches opens with the CONTENT HIDDEN. The student commits a prediction before the tool shows any result, marked answer, filled table or read out. Committing emits prediction_made, which unlocks step 1 so the real result animates in BESIDE the guess.
predict_first.scope: Step 1 only. Steps 2..N use the ordinary reveal gate: scene and question shown, answer hidden until reveal.
mechanism: a prediction state field on the shared state
a prediction_made event listed in events[]
the emit fires once per step 1, never re-asked on later steps

terminal_event.name: finished
terminal_event.note: The host treats name === 'completed' || name === 'finished' as end of activity and writes the lesson summary. Emit 'finished' exactly once, guarded by a one shot ref that only reset() re-arms; the celebration overlay and chime sit OUTSIDE the guard so a second tap re-opens them. Never emit a bare 'completed', and never name a progress event '*_completed'. Progress events are named for what happened (step_done, example_done, bank_done). The Finish button renders ONLY in practice and normal, gated on the MODE, never on operatorMode.
terminal_event.firedBy: the last item of the active bank being answered, or the student pressing Finish

practice.selection: Six served per load, one drawn at random from each slot's five item type. Composition is fixed and the specific question inside a slot is random, so repeat visits to the same tool show different questions.
practice.exclusions: Nothing shown solved in Learn is ever served here, checkpoints included. No question text repeats inside this mount. Practice values differ from the textbook's own printed problem values.
practice.source_prop: props.questions, drawn at random inside each slot's difficulty and subtype
practice.interaction_rules: At least 4 distinct interactions, none above 40 per cent, at least 2 per difficulty band, at most 4 the same inside one type of five.
practice.fallback_precedence: DIFFICULTY is fixed and never traded: a Hard slot serves a Hard question or nothing. SUBTYPE gives way second, because it decides what thinking the slot does. SOURCE gives way first, because provenance matters less than the kind of thinking.

visual_behaviour.never: Do not show the result while a sign prediction is open, and never render the trace in reading order when the structure requires otherwise. A left to right trace would teach the very error the tool exists to remove.
visual_behaviour.scene: The expression across the top with the letter highlighted wherever it appears, a value slider beneath it, and a step trace running down the panel with the operation named and the running value beside each line.
visual_behaviour.layout: Expression, slider, trace stacked. On a 390 px frame the trace scrolls within the panel and the slider keeps a 44 px thumb.
readouts: The current value of the letter, always on screen
The running value after each applied step
The exact result as a fraction, once the prediction is committed
animations: Slider move: every occurrence of the letter flashes to the new value together, which shows substitution as one simultaneous replacement.
Step: the operated part of the expression lifts and resolves into its value, so the operation is seen acting on a specific subtree.
Sign change: terms that change sign as the value crosses zero pulse once, which separates them from terms that do not.
visual_behaviour.scale_rule: The expression is scaled so every term stays readable and wraps rather than shrinking; the trace scrolls rather than compressing its lines.

teaching_sequence.rationale: The operations have to be watched acting on the parts of the expression they actually own before any rule about signs is stated, or the rule becomes one more thing to remember at the moment it is needed most

tool_config.image_prompts_note: Empty by design. This mount is a mechanism, not a depiction, and the standard mandates hand-built inline SVG with no external asset dependency, so no depictive picture is declared.
mathematical_facts: Substituting replaces every occurrence of the letter with the same number, all at once
In 3x squared the squaring acts on x alone, so at x equal to 2 the term is 12 and not 36
An even power of a negative value is positive, while an odd power keeps the sign
The order of the operations is fixed by the structure of the expression, not by the order the symbols are read

question_integration.test: Freeze any injected step and ask: could the teacher read every number in this question off THIS screen? If not, fix the scene, not the words.
question_integration.parse_rule: Read the expression and the value out of the question text and load them with the trace collapsed and the result hidden. The expression drawn must be exactly the one the question states.
question_integration.compute_rule: Build the scene from the parsed numbers, then compute the answer with the tool's own ground truth function ON THE DRAWN SCENE. Never carry the bank's answer as truth while drawing a different scene. The two must agree by construction; if they disagree the scene is wrong, not the bank.

question_integration.sceneless_rule: A general claim with no expression in it ('why does a negative value not make every term negative?') has nothing to evaluate. Render an authored, self consistent case that exhibits the claim, in this tool 3x squared plus 5x traced at minus 3, rather than fabricating an expression the question does not describe.

teaching_notes: Beat 1 exists to make the substitution VISIBLE as one act. Both copies of x flash to (-3) in the same frame and the substituted line is written with brackets, because omitting that bracket is precisely how the (-3) squared = -9 error is produced. Ask the class out loud, before landing the beat, whether 3x squared + 5x will come out positive or negative at x = -3 - the class is genuinely split, and the board settles it.

Beat 2 is the mechanism. The dashed scope box is drawn round the letter alone, and the rival reading (3x) squared stands beside it in its own column with its own value - 27 against 81. That is the whole argument: the student's 81 is not wrong arithmetic, it is the right arithmetic for a DIFFERENT expression, one that has a bracket the board does not.

Beat 3 is the consolidation and it is the one to point at. The value moves from -3 to 2 and only the terms that actually changed sign pulse: the squared term does not move, the linear term does. A whole-expression sign rule would predict every term pulsing, and the screen refuses it. Say which term changed and which did not, and read both values off the board rather than from memory.
media.generation_prompt: Substitution Machine: a value slider feeding an expression, with a step trace generated from the parsed tree so each operation is applied in structural order and can be paused and predicted
media.instructions_for_student: 1. Read the expression and find every place the letter appears. 2. Slide the value to the number you want to substitute. 3. Say whether the result will be positive or negative, and commit that prediction. 4. Step the trace one line at a time and read the running value after each operation. 5. Check which part of the expression each operation acted on. 6. Type the exact result, as a fraction if it is not a whole number. 7. Drag the value across zero and watch which terms change sign. 8. Try a value of zero and say which terms are left. 9. In Practice, answer each item and press Finish when the bank is done.

topics.summary: Carry the secret start as a letter and it cancels, forcing one ending. The same idea recovers a hidden date, because the steps build a number you can take apart.

content.text: In a 'think of a number' trick you double, add, halve, and so on, then subtract the number you first thought of. It feels like the machine must somehow read your number, because it always announces the right ending. Algebra shows there is no reading at all. Call the start x. Each step is written as an expression: double gives 2x, add 10 gives 2x plus 10, halve gives x plus 5. Notice the x is still there, but so is a fixed number. The last step, subtract the original, takes away the x and leaves only the fixed number. That number is the same whatever x was, so every starting number lands on the same ending. The trick is forced, not lucky.

content.text: In the date trick a friend takes the month and day of a secret date and runs a fixed set of steps: multiply the month by 5, add 6, multiply by 4, add 9, multiply by 5, then add the day. Writing the month as M and the day as D, the steps always build up to 100M plus 165 plus D. The 165 is fixed, and it is baked in by the recipe, not by the date. So from the reported answer you subtract 165, which leaves 100M plus D. Because the day D is at most 31, it fills the last two digit places, and the month sits in the hundreds. Reading those apart gives the date. The trick is not mind reading: the recipe forces the answer into a shape you can take apart.

topics.publication_chunk: In a 'think of a number' trick you double, add, halve, and so on, then subtract the number you first thought of. It feels like the machine must somehow read your number, because it always announces the right ending. Algebra shows there is no reading at all. Call the start x. Each step is written as an expression: double gives 2x, add 10 gives 2x plus 10, halve gives x plus 5. Notice the x is still there, but so is a fixed number. The last step, subtract the original, takes away the x and leaves only the fixed number. That number is the same whatever x was, so every starting number lands on the same ending. learning_objectives.objective_text: Students will be able to infer why a think of a number trick always announces the same ending, and determine that carrying the start as x through each step leaves x plus a fixed number before the final move. They will explain that subtracting the original number cancels the x and leaves only that fixed number, so every possible starting value lands on the identical answer and the outcome is forced rather than lucky.

Students will be able to infer why a single reported number can reveal a secret date, and determine that writing the month as M and the day as D drives the fixed steps to the form 100M plus 165 plus D. They will explain that subtracting 165 leaves 100M plus D, so the last two digits give the day and the hundreds give the month, letting any date be rebuilt from the final number alone.

media.title: Like Term Dragger
media.context: Class 8 mathematics, the chapter on expressions and equations. The tool lays out an expression as loose chips, shaped by kind and coloured by letter, with a simplified strip pinned beneath that reads back whatever the board holds and a substitution check below that evaluates any two forms at the same number. It matters because collecting like terms is the step that every later piece of work runs through, tidying the running expression of a trick, collecting the unknown onto one side of an equation, reading a rule off a pattern, and because the error it invites, adding a coefficient to a constant, is invisible in the symbols and obvious in the values. It sits after equations can be balanced and before the unknown appears on both sides, where collecting first becomes unavoidable.

overview.goal: The student combines like terms by merging chips and explains, by substituting a number, why unlike terms cannot be combined.
overview.theme: Class 8 register: clean geometric line work, one accent plus one second accent, no decoration Setting: A plain working ground carrying a board of loose term chips, shaped by kind and coloured by letter, with a simplified strip pinned along the bottom that reads back whatever the board currently holds. Character: none, because this mount is an instrument. Premise: A class claims that 3x plus 8 can be written as 11x, and one test number is asked to decide it.
overview.concept: Like terms have the same letter part and can be added by adding coefficients. Unlike terms cannot, because they count different things: 3x plus 8 stays as it is, and writing it as 11x changes the expression's value at every number except one.
overview.purpose: The student combines like terms by merging chips and explains, by substituting a number, why unlike terms cannot be combined.
overview.blackboard: Any theorem, derivation, proof, formula or numerical calculation that takes MORE THAN TWO mathematical steps is written on the blackboard step by step, one step below the previous one, in logical order. Never show all the steps at once and never combine two calculations into one line. One calculation per line.
overview.uiOverview: Board fills the main panel with the strip pinned beneath and the substitution check below that. On a 390 px frame every chip keeps a 44 px hit target and the board scrolls rather than shrinking chips. The Finish button renders ONLY in Practice and Free Play, gated positively on the mode. The HOST renders the mode selector, the language switcher and the mute in its own bar; this tool does not draw them and never lists the mode selector as a student control.
overview.neverRemove: Do not complete an illegal merge even momentarily, and never let x and x squared share a shape. A chip that briefly merges before springing back would teach that the combination is possible but discouraged.
overview.predictFirst: Step 1 of every mode that teaches opens with the CONTENT HIDDEN. The student commits a prediction before the tool shows any result, marked answer, filled table or read out. Committing emits prediction_made, which unlocks step 1 so the real result animates in BESIDE the guess.
overview.flowOfUnderstanding: Predict, then observe, then compare, then conclude. Adding coefficients is the distributive law read backwards: 3x plus 5x is (3 plus 5) times x, which needs both terms to be multiples of the same thing. There is no common factor to pull out of 3x and 8, so no single term can replace them. The substitution check makes this concrete: any legal merge leaves the value unchanged at every test number, and any illegal one changes it. Concept reveals the idea in 3 beats, Learn works the five checkpoints solved, Practice serves six drawn questions scored, and Free Play unlocks everything with nothing required.

conceptMode.teacherCallPlan: Call 1. Open with a chip for 3x sitting beside a chip for 8 and the strip reading 3x plus 8, with no merge attempted, and ask the class to say out loud whether these two can be added into one term. Commit the class verdict on the prediction pad. Targets the x chip and the unit chip. Never attempt a merge before the prediction is committed. Call 2. Drag the unlike pair together so it bounces apart, then drag a like pair together so it fuses and the coefficient counts up on the badge. Point at the refused pair and then at the merged chip. Targets the unlike pair first, then a like pair of x chips. Read the simplified strip from getState().truth, never from this plan. Call 3. Substitute the test value into the correct strip and into the wrongly combined form, and let the two values stand side by side. Targets the substitution check at a test value of 2 and the value of each form. Say which form the board agrees with, reading both values from getState().truth.

hunts: CROSSING VALUE: find a wrong merge and the one value of x where it happens to agree with the truth.
EMPTY THE KIND: build a board with four chips of one kind that leaves nothing of that kind behind.
SAME BOARD, NEW ORDER: write the simplified board three ways and check all three at one value.
SHAPE SORT: fill the trays with eight chips so that no two trays hold the same number of chips.

observationsAndConclusions.why: There is no common factor to take out of 3x and 8, so no single chip can stand for both
observationsAndConclusions.observe: An unlike pair bounces apart every time, at every place on the board
observationsAndConclusions.conclusion: Terms are combined because they count the same thing, not because they sit next to each other

observationsAndConclusions.why: Adding coefficients is the distributive law read backwards, which is an identity rather than a rearrangement
observationsAndConclusions.observe: A like merge leaves the strip's value unchanged at every test number tried
observationsAndConclusions.conclusion: A legal collection is one that changes how the expression is written and never what it is worth

observationsAndConclusions.why: Two different expressions can still cross at a single value, which one lucky test cannot tell apart
observationsAndConclusions.observe: A wrong merge can agree with the correct form at one particular test number and disagrees everywhere else
observationsAndConclusions.conclusion: One agreeing test number is not a check; the forms have to agree at every value

media.description: The student drags one chip onto another and the board answers: like chips fuse into one with the coefficient counting up on its badge, unlike chips bounce apart with a short shake and return to their places, and a chip meeting its opposite annihilates so that no zero term is left standing. The simplified strip along the bottom always reads back the board's current expression, so a collection is a change to how it is written and never to what it holds. The substitution check settles any argument: a test number is put into the student's form and into the correct one at once, and the two values are shown together, which also exposes the trap of a wrong form that happens to agree at one particular number.

scenes.valuesShown: Blackboard lines, in order: A chip's kind is its letter piece, and these two have different kinds. | Adding coefficients is the shared factor being taken outside, which needs one shared kind. | There is no shared factor in 3x and 8, so no single chip can replace them. | The chips bounce apart and stay separate on the board. scenes.valuesShown: Every readout stays live, so the invariants keep being computed while the student explores

concept.notation: A term is a coefficient and a kind, where the kind is the letter part such as x, x squared or the constant. Only terms of the same kind may be combined, by adding their coefficients.
concept.statement: Like terms have the same letter part and can be added by adding coefficients. Unlike terms cannot, because they count different things: 3x plus 8 stays as it is, and writing it as 11x changes the expression's value at every number except one.
prerequisites: a letter standing for a number
substituting a value into an expression
misconceptions: Unlike terms combined, so 3x plus 8 is written as 11x.
x and x squared treated as the same kind because they use the same letter.
A negative term's sign lost when it is collected.
concept.why_it_is_true: Adding coefficients is the distributive law read backwards: 3x plus 5x is (3 plus 5) times x, which needs both terms to be multiples of the same thing. There is no common factor to pull out of 3x and 8, so no single term can replace them. The substitution check makes this concrete: any legal merge leaves the value unchanged at every test number, and any illegal one changes it.
worked_numbers: 3x plus 5x is 8x, and at x equal to 2 both forms give 16.
3x plus 8 is not 11x: at x equal to 2 the first is 14 and the second is 22.
The pyramid top (a plus b) plus (b plus c) collects to a plus 2b plus c, since only the b terms are alike.

extra: 3x plus 5x collected on the board and checked at x equal to 2
3x plus 8 attempted as one term and refused, with the values compared at a test number
The pyramid collection a plus b added to b plus c, where only the b terms are alike
7y minus 7y, where a chip and its opposite cancel and the kind leaves the strip altogether
2x plus 3x squared, kept as two terms because the letter parts differ
4p plus 9 plus 6p plus 1, collected in a different order and checked to give the same strip
A wrong merge tested at x equal to 1, where the two forms happen to agree, then tested again elsewhere
textbook: The top entry of a number pyramid collected from its bottom row, where only the middle terms are alike
The running expression of a number trick tidied after each instruction
The total of the four entries of a calendar grid collected into 4x plus a constant
The sum of a two digit number and its reverse collected into a multiple of eleven
The difference of a two digit number and its reverse collected into a multiple of nine

chipKindOutcomes.x: a rounded chip whose coefficient counts copies of x, merging only with other x chips
chipKindOutcomes.y: a rounded chip in a second colour, which merges with y chips only and never with x chips
chipKindOutcomes.unit: a square chip carrying a plain number, which merges only with other unit chips
chipKindOutcomes.x squared: a taller chip that never merges with an x chip, since the letter parts differ

tryMergeOutcomes.like pair: the two chips slide together into one, and the new coefficient counts up on the badge
tryMergeOutcomes.unlike pair: the pair bounces apart with a short shake and both chips return to their places
tryMergeOutcomes.opposite pair: the two chips annihilate and the kind leaves the simplified strip entirely

chipsEnabledOutcomes.true: chips can be dragged and merged directly on the board
chipsEnabledOutcomes.false: the board is fixed and the simplified form has to be typed instead of dragged

answer_key.worked: (a plus b) plus (b plus c) collects to a plus 2b plus c, because only the two b terms are of the same kind.
answer_key.practice: Computed per item at runtime from the chips as laid out: the normalised term map and the value of each form at the test number.
answer_key.precision: Grading is by normalised comparison of the term map, never by string equality, so any correct ordering of the terms is accepted.
answer_key.ground_truth: normalise(expression) = a map from kind to exact coefficient. valueAt(expression, n) = the exact value. isLegalMerge(a, b) = the kinds match.

blackboard.rule: Any theorem, derivation, proof, formula or numerical calculation that takes MORE THAN TWO mathematical steps is written on the blackboard step by step, one step below the previous one, in logical order.

modes.ai: The agent narrates while the board fills; the board never runs ahead of the narration.
modes.learn: The board is the reveal. Before reveal() it is empty; on reveal it fills line by line, then the answer lands last.
modes.normal: No board unless the student asks the tool to settle something, then the same line by line fill.
modes.practice: The board stays empty until the answer is checked, then fills line by line as the explanation.

blackboard.for_a_proof: State the claim first, then write and explain each step in sequence, then close on the conclusion.
blackboard.readability: Keep the board clean and uncrowded, at Class 8 reading level, with the same symbols the scene uses.
blackboard.applies_when: The explanation runs to more than two mathematical steps. Two steps or fewer may be written together.
blackboard.for_a_calculation: Show the complete working line by line, including every intermediate value, before the final answer is shown.
blackboard.one_step_per_line: Never show all the steps at once and never combine two calculations into one line. One calculation per line.
blackboard.source_of_the_lines: The `steps` array of the Learn checkpoint or Practice question on screen IS the blackboard, in order. Render one array entry per line. It is gated at build time: no entry carries two calculations.
blackboard.builds_progressively: The board fills line by line as the explanation is given, so the student can see how each step follows from the one above it. A line already written stays on the board.

edge_cases.case: A merge attempted between unlike chips
edge_cases.tool_behaviour: Both chips bounce apart with a short shake and stay separate, with the kinds named rather than the move being completed.

edge_cases.case: A negative chip merged with its positive
edge_cases.tool_behaviour: They cancel to nothing and the strip loses that kind entirely, which the tool states rather than leaving a zero term showing.

edge_cases.case: x and x squared on the board together
edge_cases.tool_behaviour: Treated as different kinds and drawn with different shapes, so the shared letter does not suggest they combine.

edge_cases.case: A simplified answer written in a different order
edge_cases.tool_behaviour: Accepted, since grading compares normalised term maps rather than strings.

edge_cases.case: A test value where a wrong merge happens to agree
edge_cases.tool_behaviour: A second test value is offered automatically, since one agreeing case does not make the forms equal.
