shared_state.note: Exactly what getState() returns and what rides every {type:'state'} emit. The teacher agent reads these field names, so they are a contract: renaming one silently breaks narration.

aiModeCalls.steps: next() / prev() / gotoStep(index) over the Concept beats; playDemo() auto runs them all
aiModeCalls.description: In Concept the agent orchestrates the demonstration from these calls. next() / prev() / gotoStep drive the 3 built in beats; the component calls let the agent branch a beat, for example attempting the exact merge a child proposes and letting the chips refuse it.

postmessage.note: The tool emits {type:'ready', toolId} on mount and commands sent before it are DROPPED. Every windowMethod is also reachable as a command method.

agent_control.operator_note: Concept (ai) and Learn are TEACHER operated. The agent calls the step verbs and narrates; the class watches and answers out loud. No beat in these two modes may carry operate-the-control copy (no 'tap your guess', 'press Check', 'drag the marker'). Keep the thinking half of the sentence ('Predict first', 'Say your answer out loud first') and drop the device half. Practice and Free Play are student operated and address the student directly.

predict_first.rule: Step 1 of every mode that teaches opens with the CONTENT HIDDEN. The student commits a prediction before the tool shows any result, marked answer, filled table or read out. Committing emits prediction_made, which unlocks step 1 so the real result animates in BESIDE the guess.
predict_first.scope: Step 1 only. Steps 2..N use the ordinary reveal gate: scene and question shown, answer hidden until reveal.

visual_behaviour.never: Do not complete an illegal merge even momentarily, and never let x and x squared share a shape. A chip that briefly merges before springing back would teach that the combination is possible but discouraged.
visual_behaviour.scene: A board of draggable term chips, shaped by kind and coloured by letter, with unit chips square, x chips rounded and squared chips taller, and a simplified strip pinned along the bottom showing the current expression.
visual_behaviour.layout: Board fills the main panel with the strip pinned beneath and the substitution check below that. On a 390 px frame every chip keeps a 44 px hit target and the board scrolls rather than shrinking chips.
readouts: The simplified expression on the strip, always on screen
The coefficient on each merged chip
The value of each form at the test number, once a substitution is run
animations: Merge: two like chips slide together and become one, with the new coefficient counting up, so the addition is seen happening to the coefficients.
Refusal: an unlike pair bounces apart with a short shake and returns to place, which reads as impossible rather than as declined.
Cancellation: a negative chip and its positive annihilate and the kind leaves the strip, so zero terms are not left standing.
visual_behaviour.scale_rule: Chips keep a minimum readable size and the board scrolls when there are many; chips are never shrunk to fit.

teaching_sequence.rationale: The chips have to refuse an unlike merge, and a test number has to disagree with the wrong answer, before the rule about letter parts is stated, or collecting terms becomes a habit of adding whatever numbers are in sight

question_integration.test: Freeze any injected step and ask: could the teacher read every number in this question off THIS screen? If not, fix the scene, not the words.

question_integration.compute_rule: Build the scene from the parsed numbers, then compute the answer with the tool's own ground truth function ON THE DRAWN SCENE. Never carry the bank's answer as truth while drawing a different scene. The two must agree by construction; if they disagree the scene is wrong, not the bank.

teaching_notes: Beat 1 exists so the merge is a DECISION, not a rule recited. Two x chips sit on the board with the outcome hidden; ask the class to say out loud whether they can be written as one term and commit their verdict before a single chip moves.

Beat 2 is the justification in one picture, in NCERT's own words: adding coefficients is the shared kind being taken outside the bracket, 3x + 5x = (3 + 5)x. The unlike pair 3x and 8 bounces apart because there is no shared piece to take out — never call this the distributive law.

Beat 3 is where an agreeing test value is shown to prove nothing. 3x + 8 and 11x both give 11 at x = 1, and the tool offers the SECOND value automatically because one crossing is not a proof. Ask for the second value before the tool supplies it.

A unit chip is drawn a DIFFERENT SHAPE, not merely a different colour, so a child cannot read the board as 'fruit salad'; a 0x chip is never drawn, not for one frame; and the sign travels with its term (+8x and −8x, never a floating operator).
media.generation_prompt: Like Term Dragger: terms as shaped and coloured chips that merge only with their own kind, unlike pairs bouncing apart, and a strip showing the simplified expression at every moment
media.instructions_for_student: 1. Read the chips on the board and the expression on the strip beneath them. 2. Decide which chips are of the same kind. 3. Drag one chip onto another and see whether they fuse or bounce apart. 4. Read the coefficient on each merged chip. 5. Type the simplified expression in any order you like. 6. Choose a test value and substitute it into your form and into the strip. 7. Compare the two values and say whether your collection was legal. 8. Try a second test value, so one lucky agreement cannot fool you. 9. In Practice, answer each item and press Finish when the bank is done.

topics.summary: Each brick is the sum of the two below. Fill upward, work backward with a letter when the bottom is blank, and find the top instantly as a plus 2b plus c.

content.text: A number pyramid follows one rule: every brick is the sum of the two bricks directly below it. If you know the bottom row, you can build the whole pyramid. Add the first two bottom bricks to get the left middle brick, add the next pair to get the right middle brick, then add those two middle bricks to get the top. Nothing above needs to be given, because the rule pushes the numbers upward for you. A four-row pyramid works the same way, one layer at a time. Watch out: the middle bottom bricks get used in two sums each, so a change low down can spread a long way up.

content.text: Sometimes a pyramid gives you a brick high up but leaves the bottom blank, so you cannot just add upward. Algebra fixes this. Name an unknown bottom brick with a letter, say c. Build the bricks above it as usual, but now they are expressions: if the bottom corners are 9 and 5 and the middle is c, the middle bricks are 9 plus c and c plus 5, and the top is 14 plus 2c. Setting that equal to the given top makes one equation in one letter, which you solve. Notice the blank brick appears twice, as a plus 2c term, because it feeds both middle bricks. That is why subtracting it only once gives the wrong answer.

content.text: Write the bottom row of a three-row pyramid as a, b, c. The middle bricks are a plus b and b plus c. Adding them gives the top: (a plus b) plus (b plus c), which is a plus 2b plus c. The middle brick b shows up twice, because it sits under both middle bricks, so it is doubled in the top. The corners a and c are each used once. This is why the top is not the plain total a plus b plus c. You can find any top instantly by doubling the middle value and adding the two corners. For a four-row pyramid the weights become 1, 3, 3, 1, so the two inner bricks count three times each.

topics.brief_summary: Each brick is the sum of the two below. Fill upward, work backward with a letter when the bottom is blank, and find the top instantly as a plus 2b plus c.
topics.original_chunk: A number pyramid follows one rule: every brick is the sum of the two bricks directly below it. If you know the bottom row, you can build the whole pyramid. Add the first two bottom bricks to get the left middle brick, add the next pair to get the right middle brick, then add those two middle bricks to get the top. Nothing above needs to be given, because the rule pushes the numbers upward for you. A four-row pyramid works the same way, one layer at a time. Watch out: the middle bottom bricks get used in two sums each, so a change low down can spread a long way up. Worked examples of building a pyramid from the bottom, demonstrated one step at a time across different cases. A number pyramid follows one rule: every brick is the sum of the two bricks directly below it. If you know the bottom row, you can build the whole pyramid. Add the first two bottom bricks to get the left middle brick, add the next pair to get the right middle brick, then add those two middle bricks to get the top. Nothing above needs to be given, because the rule pushes the numbers upward for you. A four-row pyramid works the same way, one layer at a time. Watch out: the middle bottom bricks get used in two sums each, so a change low down can spread a long way up. Sometimes a pyramid gives you a brick high up but leaves the bottom blank, so you cannot just add upward. Algebra fixes this. Name an unknown bottom brick with a letter, say c. Build the bricks above it as usual, but now they are expressions: if the bottom corners are 9 and 5 and the middle is c, the middle bricks are 9 plus c and c plus 5, and the top is 14 plus 2c. Setting that equal to the given top makes one equation in one letter, which you solve. Notice the blank brick appears twice, as a plus 2c term, because it feeds both middle bricks. That is why subtracting it only once gives the wrong answer. Worked examples of working a pyramid backward, demonstrated one step at a time across different cases. Sometimes a pyramid gives you a brick high up but leaves the bottom blank, so you cannot just add upward. Algebra fixes this. Name an unknown bottom brick with a letter, say c. Build the bricks above it as usual, but now they are expressions: if the bottom corners are 9 and 5 and the middle is c, the middle bricks are 9 plus c and c plus 5, and the top is 14 plus 2c. Setting that equal to the given top makes one equation in one letter, which you solve. Notice the blank brick appears twice, as a plus 2c term, because it feeds both middle bricks. That is why subtracting it only once gives the wrong answer. Write the bottom row of a three-row pyramid as a, b, c. The middle bricks are a plus b and b plus c. Adding them gives the top: (a plus b) plus (b plus c), which is a plus 2b plus c. The middle brick b shows up twice, because it sits under both middle bricks, so it is doubled in the top. The corners a and c are each used once. This is why the top is not the plain total a plus b plus c. You can find any top instantly by doubling the middle value and adding the two corners. For a four-row pyramid the weights become 1, 3, 3, 1, so the two inner bricks count three times each. Worked examples of the top as a plus 2b plus c, demonstrated one step at a time across different cases. Write the bottom row of a three-row pyramid as a, b, c. The middle bricks are a plus b and b plus c. Adding them gives the top: (a plus b) plus (b plus c), which is a plus 2b plus c. The middle brick b shows up twice, because it sits under both middle bricks, so it is doubled in the top. The corners a and c are each used once. This is why the top is not the plain total a plus b plus c. You can find any top instantly by doubling the middle value and adding the two corners. For a four-row pyramid the weights become 1, 3, 3, 1, so the two inner bricks count three times each.

learning_objectives.objective_text: Students will be able to infer how a whole number pyramid grows from its bottom row, and determine that every brick equals the sum of the two bricks directly below it, so a three-row base yields two middle bricks and one top brick. They will explain that nothing above needs to be given because the rule pushes values upward, and that a middle bottom brick feeds two sums, so a small change low down can spread far up.

Students will be able to infer how a pyramid with a blank bottom can still be completed, and determine that naming a blank bottom brick with a letter turns a given brick above into one equation in that letter. They will explain that solving it pins the missing value, and that the blank brick appears twice as a 2c term because it feeds both middle bricks, so subtracting it only once gives the wrong answer.

Students will be able to infer why the top of a three-row pyramid is not the plain total of its bottom row, and determine that writing the base as a, b, c makes the top equal a plus 2b plus c. They will explain that the middle brick b sits under both middle bricks and so is doubled while the corners a and c count once, and that a four-row base shifts the weights to 1, 3, 3, 1.
Examine the worked examples of the top as a plus 2b plus c, across different cases.
Examine the practised examples and practice questions involving the top as a plus 2b plus c, across different cases.

media.title: Recovering a calendar block from its sum
media.context: On a calendar, dates rise by 1 along a row and by 7 down a column, so a 2 by 2 block is fixed by its top left date. The worked example has a block with top left date 8 and asks for all four dates and their sum. The figure builds the block from a and totals.

media.teaching_notes: Derive each date from the top left rather than reading them off. Ask what the sum formula tells you about recovering the block from its total. Then give a sum and have students find the block.
media.negative_prompt: photorealistic rendering, photographic texture, 3D modelling, isometric or perspective projection, drop shadows, gradients, glossy or metallic surfaces, neon glow; decorative clutter, background scenery, ornamental borders, frames, mascots, emoji, speech bubbles that carry no information; watermarks, signatures, logos, stock imagery, colour swatches; garbled or misspelled words, invented digits, duplicated or contradictory labels, handwriting and script fonts, wording in any script other than English; text cropped at the edge, labels overlapping the figure, type too small to read at half size; any wording at all beyond the listed labels, including added titles, captions, summaries, or a sentence describing what the figure shows; a calendar row length other than seven; a date that does not follow from the step arrows; a sum that does not match the four dates; a general formula that does not simplify correctly; a block that is not 2 by 2
media.generation_prompt: Flat educational vector illustration in the style of an NCERT Grade 8 mathematics textbook: plain white background, thin uniform dark outlines, a restrained palette of one teal accent, one amber accent and neutral grey, flat fills with no shading and no gradients, all wording in a clean sans-serif, 16:9 landscape at 1456 by 816 pixels. Scene: A calendar grid is drawn with a 2 by 2 block outlined in bold teal, its top left cell holding 8. Two step arrows label the moves: rightward adds 1 and downward adds 7. The four cells are filled as 8, 9, 15 and 16, each with its expression written beneath in letters as a, a plus 1, a plus 7 and a plus 8. An addition strip reads '8 + 9 + 15 + 16 = 48', with a general strip reading 'a + (a + 1) + (a + 7) + (a + 8) = 4a + 16' and a substitution check reading '4 x 8 + 16 = 48'. A note reads that the whole block follows from one date. Draw no wording at all except the following, which is the complete and only text in the figure, spelled exactly like this: 8; 9; 15; 16; rightward adds 1; downward adds 7; a; a + 1; a + 7; a + 8; 8 + 9 + 15 + 16 = 48; 4a + 16; 4 x 8 + 16 = 48.
media.accuracy_constraints:
The calendar must have seven days in each row, so a downward step adds 7.
The four dates must be 8, 9, 15 and 16, matching a, a plus 1, a plus 7 and a plus 8.
The sum must be 48, matching 4a plus 16 at a equal to 8.
The block must be exactly 2 by 2.
Every date must follow from the top left by the stated steps.
Every number, count and label drawn in the figure must match this brief exactly; no value may be invented, rounded or added.
Use NCERT Ganita Prakash Grade 8 wording for every term, keep British spelling, and write no sentence that a Grade 8 reader could not read aloud.

media.title: Word Problem Modeller
media.context: CBSE Class 8, NCERT Ganita Prakash Part 2 'Algebra Play' (calendar 2x2 blocks and number pyramids), resting on Linear Equations in One Variable. The class has met variable, term, coefficient, equation, LHS/RHS, transposing and verification; it has NOT met function, parameter, domain or 'linear model'. The tape/bar diagram is not itself an NCERT Class 8 figure, so it is drawn self-explaining and labelled 'not to scale' until it is solved. Every worked line is one operation, never chained, and every answer closes with the mandated sentence.

finish.normal: The same panel with no star and evaluated false. There is no play again loop.
finish.practice: A full screen celebration carrying a star rating from the real score, all correct 3, 60 per cent or more 2, else 1 and never 0, plus a what you have learned panel and Review. The star screen offers Review, which walks every item showing the student's unknown, tape, equation and sentence against a canonical model.
whatYouLearned: Modelling starts by naming what the letter stands for, in words, before anything is written

overview.goal: The student models a word problem as an equation, solves it, and interprets the solution as a sentence about the situation with units.
overview.theme: Class 8 register: clean geometric line work, one accent plus one second accent, no decoration Setting: A plain working ground carrying the problem in words across the top, a tape of labelled segments beneath it and a working column down the side that ends in a sentence rather than a number. Character: none, because this mount is an instrument. Premise: A class is given the total of four entries in a calendar grid and asked to recover the entries themselves.
overview.concept: Modelling a word problem means choosing what the letter stands for, expressing the story's quantities in terms of it, and writing the equality the story asserts. Solving gives a number, and the number only becomes an answer when it is read back into the situation with its units.
overview.purpose: The student models a word problem as an equation, solves it, and interprets the solution as a sentence about the situation with units.
overview.blackboard: Any theorem, derivation, proof, formula or numerical calculation that takes MORE THAN TWO mathematical steps is written on the blackboard step by step, one step below the previous one, in logical order. Never show all the steps at once and never combine two calculations into one line. One calculation per line.
overview.uiOverview: Problem, tape, working stacked. On a 390 px frame the tape keeps full width, segments keep a 44 px hit target and the working column scrolls. The Finish button renders ONLY in Practice and Free Play, gated positively on the mode. The HOST renders the mode selector, the language switcher and the mute in its own bar; this tool does not draw them and never lists the mode selector as a student control.
overview.neverRemove: Do not block a wrong tape when it is built, and never accept a bare number as the answer to a story problem. Blocking early would hide the inconsistency that teaches the check.
overview.predictFirst: Step 1 of every mode that teaches opens with the CONTENT HIDDEN. The student commits a prediction before the tool shows any result, marked answer, filled table or read out. Committing emits prediction_made, which unlocks step 1 so the real result animates in BESIDE the guess.
overview.flowOfUnderstanding: Predict, then observe, then compare, then conclude. The equation is a translation, and a translation is only faithful if each part of it corresponds to something in the story. The tape makes the correspondence visible: if the tape does not match the story's constraints, the equation built from it will not either, and the mismatch appears at the check stage rather than being ruled out in advance. Reading the solution back with units closes the loop, since the same number can answer different questions in the same story. Concept reveals the idea in 3 beats, Learn works the five checkpoints solved, Practice serves six drawn questions scored, and Free Play unlocks everything with nothing required.

learnMode.summary: Learn, teacher operated. The worked items arrive in props.learnQuestions, mandatory checkpoints first. Each item loads its own problem, poses the modelling question, then reveals the tape, the equation, the solution and the sentence together as one beat. Prev / Next move between items.
learnMode.checkpointPlan: ML1 (Easy, Edge Case): A solved equation returns a number, and the number becomes an answer only when it is named with its unit. Breaks: A numeric answer given without interpretation. ML2 (Medium, Edge Case): The choice of unknown is free, and the check is whether the equation matches the story it came from. Breaks: Believing one situation has only one correct equation. ML3 (Medium, Conceptual): An equation is only an answer to the story it faithfully translates, and the check is where a mismatch appears. Breaks: Believing any equation that produces a number has answered the question. ML4 (Hard, Edge Case): A fractional solution in a counting situation is a statement about the situation, not an invitation to round. Breaks: Rounding a fractional solution to make a counting situation come out. ML5 (Hard, Edge Case): The letter may name any quantity in the story, so the asked quantity is not automatically the best choice. Breaks: The unknown chosen as the quantity asked for even when another choice makes the equation simpler.

conceptMode.teacherCallPlan: Call 1. Open on the calendar grid problem with a blank tape and no quantity marked, and ask the class to say out loud which quantity they would call x. Commit the class choice on the prediction pad. Targets the problem text and the markable quantities. Never build the tape before the prediction is committed. Call 2. Mark that quantity, let its segment appear on the tape, and build the remaining segments from it so the total bracket closes over the whole strip, then write the equation beside it. Point at the tape and then at the equation line. Targets the marked unknown, the four segments and the equation line. Read the equation from getState().truth, never from this plan. Call 3. Solve the equation and then turn the number into a sentence about the situation, with what it counts and its units attached. Targets the solve steps and the answer sentence. Read the solution from getState().truth and say the sentence in full.

observationsAndConclusions.why: The letter names a quantity in the story rather than the answer, so any faithful naming describes the same situation
observationsAndConclusions.observe: Two students who call different quantities x end up writing different equations and reaching the same block of entries
observationsAndConclusions.conclusion: There is no single correct choice of unknown; there are faithful choices and unfaithful ones

observationsAndConclusions.why: The tape is drawn from the model that has actually been built, never from the intended answer
observationsAndConclusions.observe: A tape that disagrees with the story shakes at the exact segment that disagrees
observationsAndConclusions.conclusion: A model that returns a number is not thereby correct, which is why the tape is checked before it is solved

observationsAndConclusions.why: The same number can answer several different questions about one situation, so the question has to be named
observationsAndConclusions.observe: The working stops at a number and the panel still asks for one more line
observationsAndConclusions.conclusion: An answer carries what it counts and its units, which is what turns 16 into the top left entry is 16

media.description: A word problem sits across the top of the frame and a tape of labelled segments is drawn beneath it: identical boxes for the equal unknowns, a numbered box for each constant, a reduction drawn as a notch cut off the end, and one brace across the whole strip. Before the solve the strip is SCHEMATIC and says so, because an unknown box drawn at its solved width leaks the answer; the moment the equation is solved the same strip redraws TO SCALE against the story's own total mark, so a faithful model visibly closes on the mark and an unfaithful one visibly overshoots it and shakes. Every width in either regime comes from ONE layout function that returns viewBox units per story unit and the width of one unknown box, so the drawn position, the printed read-out and the graded answer can never disagree. The equation is read off the completed tape, solved as an exact fraction (a count that comes out 7/2 stays 7/2 and is named as impossible rather than rounded), and the working column ends in a sentence that names the quantity and its unit rather than in a bare number. Concept walks the calendar block in three beats, Learn shows five reviewed checkpoints already answered, Practice serves six drawn questions on a difficulty ladder with a Review pass, and Free Play opens every stage at once.

scenes.onScreen: The problem field, the tape, the equation line, the solve strip, the sentence box, every control, no score and no question. An editable problem with every stage open at once.

concept.notation: The unknown is named explicitly, for example x is the number of dates in the block. A tape segment of unknown length stands for x and labelled segments stand for the known amounts.
concept.statement: Modelling a word problem means choosing what the letter stands for, expressing the story's quantities in terms of it, and writing the equality the story asserts. Solving gives a number, and the number only becomes an answer when it is read back into the situation with its units.
prerequisites: writing an expression for a described quantity
misconceptions: The unknown chosen as the quantity asked for even when another choice makes the equation simpler.
A numeric answer given without interpretation, so 4 is offered where 4 dates was asked for.
concept.why_it_is_true: The equation is a translation, and a translation is only faithful if each part of it corresponds to something in the story. The tape makes the correspondence visible: if the tape does not match the story's constraints, the equation built from it will not either, and the mismatch appears at the check stage rather than being ruled out in advance. Reading the solution back with units closes the loop, since the same number can answer different questions in the same story.
worked_numbers: Four dates in a calendar block sum to 80. Taking x as the top left date the block is x, x plus 1, x plus 7 and x plus 8, so 4x plus 16 equal to 80.
Solving gives x equal to 16, so the block is 16, 17, 23 and 24.
The answer is the top left date is 16, not simply 16.

extra: A three by one strip of a calendar whose entries add to a given total
A block modelled from its bottom right entry instead of its top left, giving a different equation
A problem where the tape is built wrongly and still returns a number, caught at the check stage
A cost problem whose answer needs rupees attached before it means anything
A sharing problem whose solution is not a whole number, in a situation that counts objects
A problem solved with the tape stage removed, once three tapes have been built correctly
A problem whose answer is the number of the second quantity rather than the one called x
textbook: The calendar grid puzzle: the four entries of a two by two block add to a given total and the entries have to be found
The same block written from its top left entry as x, x plus 1, x plus 7 and x plus 8
The equation for that block collected and solved for the top left entry
The bottom row of a number pyramid recovered from a stated top entry
The two digit number recovered after its reverse is subtracted and the difference is given

markUnknownOutcomes.the total: the tool refuses the choice and says so, since the total is already given and naming it leaves nothing unknown
markUnknownOutcomes.top left entry: the other three segments become x plus 1, x plus 7 and x plus 8, and the equation collects to 4x plus a constant
markUnknownOutcomes.bottom right entry: the other three segments are written by subtraction, giving a faithful equation with a different constant
markUnknownOutcomes.the number asked for: a legal choice that is sometimes the harder one, and the tape is built from it exactly as written

tapeSegmentOutcomes.unknown: one segment of unmeasured length, drawn the same width wherever it appears
tapeSegmentOutcomes.a known amount: a labelled block whose width is drawn to its stated value
tapeSegmentOutcomes.unknown plus a constant: an unknown segment with a labelled block attached to its end
tapeSegmentOutcomes.a multiple of the unknown: that many unknown segments laid end to end, all of one width

answer_key.worked: Four dates summing to 80 give 4x plus 16 equal to 80, so x equal to 16, and the answer sentence is that the top left date is 16.
answer_key.practice: Computed per item at runtime from the item's problem: the unknown definition, the canonical equation, the exact solution and the required units.
answer_key.precision: The equation is graded by normalised equivalence so any valid modelling choice passes, and the units are checked as a separate field from the number.
answer_key.ground_truth: unknownOf(problem) = the accepted definitions. equationOf(problem) = the canonical equation and its equivalents. solve(equation) = the exact value. unitsOf(problem) = the required units.

blackboard.rule: Any theorem, derivation, proof, formula or numerical calculation that takes MORE THAN TWO mathematical steps is written on the blackboard step by step, one step below the previous one, in logical order.

modes.ai: The agent narrates while the board fills; the board never runs ahead of the narration.
modes.learn: The board is the reveal. Before reveal() it is empty; on reveal it fills line by line, then the answer lands last.
modes.normal: No board unless the student asks the tool to settle something, then the same line by line fill.
modes.practice: The board stays empty until the answer is checked, then fills line by line as the explanation.

blackboard.for_a_proof: State the claim first, then write and explain each step in sequence, then close on the conclusion.
blackboard.readability: Keep the board clean and uncrowded, at Class 8 reading level, with the same symbols the scene uses.
blackboard.applies_when: The explanation runs to more than two mathematical steps. Two steps or fewer may be written together.
blackboard.for_a_calculation: Show the complete working line by line, including every intermediate value, before the final answer is shown.
blackboard.one_step_per_line: Never show all the steps at once and never combine two calculations into one line. One calculation per line.
blackboard.source_of_the_lines: The `steps` array of the Learn checkpoint or Practice question on screen IS the blackboard, in order. Render one array entry per line. It is gated at build time: no entry carries two calculations.
blackboard.builds_progressively: The board fills line by line as the explanation is given, so the student can see how each step follows from the one above it. A line already written stays on the board.

edge_cases.case: A different but valid choice of unknown
edge_cases.tool_behaviour: Accepted, with the resulting equation graded on its own terms rather than against the canonical choice.

edge_cases.case: A wrong tape that still gives a number
edge_cases.tool_behaviour: Followed through to the check stage where the inconsistency with the story becomes visible, rather than being blocked when it is built.

edge_cases.case: A correct number with no units
edge_cases.tool_behaviour: Marked incomplete, since an unlabelled number is not an answer to a story problem.

edge_cases.case: A solution that is not a whole number in a counting context
edge_cases.tool_behaviour: The tool asks whether the answer can be a fraction here, which turns the arithmetic back into a question about the situation.

edge_cases.case: The tape stage removed after three successes
edge_cases.tool_behaviour: The equation stage takes the story directly and the same checks still run, so the scaffold fades without the grading weakening.

aiModeCalls.description: In Concept the agent orchestrates the demonstration from these calls. next() / prev() / gotoStep drive the 3 built in beats; the component calls let the agent branch a beat, for example taking the unknown a child names and building the tape that choice produces.

postmessage.note: The tool emits {type:'ready', toolId} on mount and commands sent before it are DROPPED. Every windowMethod is also reachable as a command method.

agent_control.operator_note: Concept (ai) and Learn are TEACHER operated. The agent calls the step verbs and narrates; the class watches and answers out loud. No beat in these two modes may carry operate-the-control copy (no 'tap your guess', 'press Check', 'drag the marker'). Keep the thinking half of the sentence ('Predict first', 'Say your answer out loud first') and drop the device half. Practice and Free Play are student operated and address the student directly.

predict_first.rule: Step 1 of every mode that teaches opens with the CONTENT HIDDEN. The student commits a prediction before the tool shows any result, marked answer, filled table or read out. Committing emits prediction_made, which unlocks step 1 so the real result animates in BESIDE the guess.
predict_first.scope: Step 1 only. Steps 2..N use the ordinary reveal gate: scene and question shown, answer hidden until reveal.
mechanism: a prediction state field on the shared state
a prediction_made event listed in events[]
the emit fires once per step 1, never re-asked on later steps

terminal_event.name: finished
terminal_event.note: The host treats name === 'completed' || name === 'finished' as end of activity and writes the lesson summary. Emit 'finished' exactly once, guarded by a one shot ref that only reset() re-arms; the celebration overlay and chime sit OUTSIDE the guard so a second tap re-opens them. Never emit a bare 'completed', and never name a progress event '*_completed'. Progress events are named for what happened (step_done, example_done, bank_done). The Finish button renders ONLY in practice and normal, gated on the MODE, never on operatorMode.
terminal_event.firedBy: the last item of the active bank being answered, or the student pressing Finish

practice.selection: Six served per load, one drawn at random from each slot's five item type. Composition is fixed and the specific question inside a slot is random, so repeat visits to the same tool show different questions.
practice.exclusions: Nothing shown solved in Learn is ever served here, checkpoints included. No question text repeats inside this mount. Practice values differ from the textbook's own printed problem values.
practice.source_prop: props.questions, drawn at random inside each slot's difficulty and subtype
practice.interaction_rules: At least 4 distinct interactions, none above 40 per cent, at least 2 per difficulty band, at most 4 the same inside one type of five.
practice.fallback_precedence: DIFFICULTY is fixed and never traded: a Hard slot serves a Hard question or nothing. SUBTYPE gives way second, because it decides what thinking the slot does. SOURCE gives way first, because provenance matters less than the kind of thinking.

visual_behaviour.never: Do not block a wrong tape when it is built, and never accept a bare number as the answer to a story problem. Blocking early would hide the inconsistency that teaches the check.
visual_behaviour.scene: The problem text across the top with markable quantities, a tape diagram beneath it made of labelled segments and one unknown segment, and a working column carrying the equation, the solve steps and the answer sentence.
visual_behaviour.layout: Problem, tape, working stacked. On a 390 px frame the tape keeps full width, segments keep a 44 px hit target and the working column scrolls.
readouts: The stated definition of the unknown, once marked
The exact solution and the required units, at the interpretation stage
animations: Marking: the chosen quantity highlights in the text and its segment appears on the tape, which ties the letter to the story.
Tape build: segments snap into a single strip whose total is shown, so the equation is read off a picture rather than guessed.
Check: a tape that contradicts the story shakes at the offending segment, which locates the fault rather than only reporting one.
visual_behaviour.scale_rule: The tape is scaled so the full strip fits with every segment at least 20 px wide; the scale adjusts rather than segments overlapping.

teaching_sequence.rationale: The tape has to be built from the student's own choice of unknown before the equation is written, or the equation arrives as a guessed arrangement of the numbers in the problem

tool_config.image_prompts_note: Empty by design. This mount is a mechanism, not a depiction, and the standard mandates hand-built inline SVG with no external asset dependency, so no depictive picture is declared.
mathematical_facts: Modelling means choosing what the letter stands for and saying so before anything is written
Each part of the equation must correspond to something in the story, which the tape makes visible
Solving gives a number; the answer is that number read back into the situation with its units
A different but faithful choice of unknown gives a different equation with the same answer

question_integration.test: Freeze any injected step and ask: could the teacher read every number in this question off THIS screen? If not, fix the scene, not the words.
question_integration.parse_rule: Read the word problem out of the question text and load it with the tape blank and no unknown marked. The quantities markable in the text must be exactly those the problem names.
question_integration.compute_rule: Build the scene from the parsed numbers, then compute the answer with the tool's own ground truth function ON THE DRAWN SCENE. Never carry the bank's answer as truth while drawing a different scene. The two must agree by construction; if they disagree the scene is wrong, not the bank.

teaching_notes: Beat 1 exists so the letter is a DECISION, not a given. The block is four cells and any one of them could be x; the beat marks the top-left, writes the other three in terms of it, and says out loud what the letter names before a single segment is added. Ask the class which cell they would have chosen before you land the beat.

Beat 2 is the whole justification in one picture. The four segments are laid end to end and the brace closes over the strip, so 4x + 16 = 80 is READ off a drawing rather than guessed from the numbers in the sentence. Point at the +1, the +7 and the +8 as separate notches: that is where 'three equal boxes leave the brace 3 short' is prevented.

Beat 3 is where an unlabelled number is shown to be incomplete. The strip goes to scale and closes exactly on the 80 mark, and only then is 16 turned into 'the top-left date is 16'. The block 16, 17, 23, 24 is the check: read all four back and add them out loud.

media.instructions_for_student: 1. Read the problem and find the quantity you are asked for. 2. Tap a quantity to mark it as the unknown, and say in words what your letter stands for. 3. Build the tape, one segment at a time, from that choice. 4. Check that the tape says what the problem says. 5. Type the equation the tape shows. 6. Solve the equation and read the exact solution. 7. Type the answer as a sentence about the situation, with its units. 8. Try the same problem again with a different quantity called x. 9. In Practice, answer each item and press Finish when the bank is done.

labels: start with a row using only one shape
media.context: In a shape grid each picture stands for a hidden number, and a row using only one kind of shape has a single unknown and can be solved. The worked example has a row reading star plus star equals 18. The figure solves that row and uses the value elsewhere.

media.teaching_notes: Hunt for the row with a single kind of shape before touching anything else. Build a key as values are found. Then substitute back into every row as the check.
media.negative_prompt: photorealistic rendering, photographic texture, 3D modelling, isometric or perspective projection, drop shadows, gradients, glossy or metallic surfaces, neon glow; decorative clutter, background scenery, ornamental borders, frames, mascots, emoji, speech bubbles that carry no information; watermarks, signatures, logos, stock imagery, colour swatches; garbled or misspelled words, invented digits, duplicated or contradictory labels, handwriting and script fonts, wording in any script other than English; text cropped at the edge, labels overlapping the figure, type too small to read at half size; any wording at all beyond the listed labels, including added titles, captions, summaries, or a sentence describing what the figure shows; a row solved that has two unknowns; a shape given two different values; a total that does not match its row; a check that fails on any row; a key entry that contradicts the grid
media.generation_prompt: Flat educational vector illustration in the style of an NCERT Grade 8 mathematics textbook: plain white background, thin uniform dark outlines, a restrained palette of one teal accent, one amber accent and neutral grey, flat fills with no shading and no gradients, all wording in a clean sans-serif, 16:9 landscape at 1456 by 816 pixels. Scene: A shape grid is drawn with rows of pictures and a total cell at the end of each row. The row reading star plus star equals 18 is picked out in teal, with a solving strip beneath reading '2 stars = 18' then 'one star = 9', and the value 9 written onto a star key at the side. A second row is then worked, containing one star and one other shape with its own total, with the known star value substituted in and the second shape solved, its value added to the key. A method note reads that a row using only one kind of shape has a single unknown and is the place to start, and a check panel substitutes both values back into every row. Draw no wording at all except the following, which is the complete and only text in the figure, spelled exactly like this: star + star = 18; 2 stars = 18; one star = 9; the key; substitute the known star; solve the second shape; start with a row using only one shape; check every row.
media.accuracy_constraints:
The starting row must contain only one kind of shape, giving a single unknown.
Each star must be 9, from 2 stars equal to 18.
Every shape must carry one value throughout the grid.
The second shape must be solved by substituting the known star value.
The check must confirm every row's total.
Every number, count and label drawn in the figure must match this brief exactly; no value may be invented, rounded or added.
Use NCERT Ganita Prakash Grade 8 wording for every term, keep British spelling, and write no sentence that a Grade 8 reader could not read aloud.

media.title: Four dates hiding as one
media.context: This hook opens the topic on recovering a calendar block from its sum. Students know the pyramid result. The film must not state the relationship between the four dates and must not recover any block.
media.description: Draw a small two by two square anywhere on a calendar and add its four dates. Tell a friend only that total and they can name all four dates at once, which seems impossible since four numbers were squeezed into one.
media.teaching_notes: Learning objective: Recover a calendar block from the sum of its entries, using the structure of the grid. Key teaching points: 1) The four dates in a block are fixed distances apart. 2) Naming the top left date fixes the other three. 3) So the total depends on one value only. 4) Solving for that value recovers the whole block. Common misconceptions: 1) Students often treat the four dates as four independent unknowns. 2) Students often forget that a calendar row is seven days long. Pause points: 0:23, at the end of and back come all four: ask how the other three dates relate to the first. 0:23, just before the open question: ask how many unknowns there really are. Questions to ask: before viewing, ask what the four dates have in common. After viewing, ask what the total would be for a block starting at nine.
media.generation_prompt:
INTENT
    Squeeze four numbers into one and get all four back, without saying how.

  STORY
    A calendar block is reported as a single total and comes back complete.

  RENDERER
    Manim Community Edition v0.18 or later. Scene subclass.
    1920x1080, 16:9, 30 fps. Default frame is 14.22 x 8 units. All content
    inside a 4 percent safe margin. Nothing cropped.

  CHAPTER VISUAL LANGUAGE, repeat verbatim in every video of this chapter
    Background: dark slate #1F2937.
    Primary object / first set: teal #0072B2.
    Secondary object / second set: amber #E69F00.
    Shared or agreeing: green #009E73.
    Focus or highlight: reddish purple #CC79A7.
    Neutral construction lines, axes, ticks: grey #6B7280.
    Wrong, rejected or impossible case only: muted red #D55E00.
    Text off white. Body 36 px equivalent, labels 28 px.
    Prose uses Text. Mathematics uses MathTex with standard LaTeX only.
    Flat fills, uniform line weights, no gradients or glow.

  ASSETS
    No external files. No image, SVG, font or audio imports. Build everything
    from Manim primitives: Line, Arc, Circle, Polygon, Dot, Arrow, Brace,
    NumberLine, Axes, Table, VGroup.

  MATHEMATICAL TRUTH MODEL
    Every value below is the only value that may appear on screen.
    the block: a two by two square anywhere on a calendar
    what is reported: the total of its four dates
    what the friend does: names all four dates at once
    why it seems impossible: four numbers were squeezed into one
    the claim: the dates are not really four separate mysteries
    withheld: the link between the four dates, and which single value controls the block

  SCENE PLAN
    Total running time 35 seconds across 3 scenes.

    Scene 1. Four dates, one total
      Duration: 12 seconds.
      On screen at the start: an empty dark slate frame.
      Beats:
      at 0.2 s  Write(s1_caption) over 0.9 s, to set the frame of the scene.
      at 2.1 s  Create(s1_grid) over 1.6 s, lag_ratio 0.06, to build the array square by square.
      at 4.7 s  FadeIn(s1_shaded) over 1.1 s, lag_ratio 0.12, to fill the cells that are being counted.
      at 6.8 s  Write(s1_glabel) over 0.8 s, to name the array.
      at 8.6 s  FadeIn(s1_gnote) over 0.8 s, to state the observation the scene has just made.
      at 10.4 s  FadeOut(s1_grid, s1_shaded, s1_glabel, s1_gnote) over 0.6 s, lag_ratio 0.05, to clear the frame, keeping only what carries on.
      Narration: "Draw a small two by two square anywhere you like on a calendar and add up its four dates. Tell a friend only that total."
      Persists into the next scene: s1_caption.

    Scene 2. And back come all four
      Duration: 11 seconds.
      On screen at the start: s1_caption.
      Beats:
      at 0.2 s  ReplacementTransform(s1_caption, s2_caption) over 0.9 s, to carry the caption forward rather than redrawing it.
      at 2.0 s  FadeIn(s2_sub) over 0.9 s, to state the situation.
      at 3.8 s  Indicate(s2_sub) over 0.8 s, to press on the surprising part.
      at 5.5 s  FadeIn(s2_lines) over 1.4 s, lag_ratio 0.35, to lay the observations down one under another.
      at 7.8 s  FadeIn(s2_note) over 0.8 s, to state the observation the scene has just made.
      at 9.5 s  FadeOut(s2_sub, s2_lines, s2_note) over 0.6 s, lag_ratio 0.05, to clear the frame, keeping only what carries on.
      Narration: "And they can name all four of those dates at once, which seems impossible, since four separate numbers were squeezed down into a single one."
      Persists into the next scene: s2_caption.

    Scene 3. The open question
      Duration: 12 seconds.
      On screen at the start: s2_caption.
      Beats:
      at 0.2 s  AddTextLetterByLetter(s3_question) over 1.8 s, to let the question land word by word.
      at 3.8 s  Create(s3_rule) over 0.6 s, to underline the question.
      at 6.2 s  FadeIn(s3_qsub) over 0.7 s, to name where the student will go looking.
      at 8.8 s  Circumscribe(s3_question) over 1.4 s, to hold the question as the closing image.
      Narration: "Yet the dates are not really four separate mysteries at all. So what links them, and which single value controls the whole block? Try the Grid Detective."
      Persists into the next scene: nothing, this is the last scene.

  ANIMATION RULES
    Prefer animation over narration wherever a concept can be shown.
    Every scene contains at least one transformation that carries meaning.
    No scene holds a static frame for more than 3 seconds.
    Reveal progressively; never dump a finished diagram in one Create.
    On-screen text minimal; no paragraph of prose on screen at any time.
    Objects that persist across scenes are transformed, never recreated.
    No decorative-only animation.

  MATHEMATICAL ACCURACY, highest priority
    100 percent accurate to NCERT Ganita Prakash for Class 8. Correct
    notation, terminology, symbols and labels as used in the Class 8
    textbook. Proportions true wherever proportion carries meaning; if a
    figure is not to scale it must say so on screen. No transformation may
    pass through a mathematically false intermediate state.

  LANGUAGE
    British spelling. No em dash and no en dash anywhere, in narration or on
    screen. Readable aloud by a student of this grade. Indian names and places
    for any person or setting.

  NEGATIVE CONSTRAINTS
    No value, label or claim absent from the truth model.
    No revealing of the rule, formula or answer anywhere in this hook.
    No worked solution, no general statement of the method.
    No text outside the safe margin, no overlapping labels.
    No external assets, watermarks or branding.
    No particles, sparkles or glow.

  SELF-CHECK BEFORE OUTPUT
    1. Scene durations sum to exactly 35 seconds across 3 scenes.
    2. Every number, count and label on screen appears in the truth model and nowhere else.
    3. Every mobject named in a beat is declared in the inventory before it is used.
    4. Every persisting mobject is transformed into its next form, never recreated.
    5. No scene holds a static frame for more than 3 seconds.
    6. All geometry lies within x in [-6.8, 6.8] and y in [-3.8, 3.8]; nothing is cropped.
    7. No label overlaps another label; buff at least 0.2 everywhere.
    8. British spelling throughout, and no em dash or en dash in narration or on screen.
    9. The final frame is the open question, with no rule, method or answer shown.
    10. The named tool is handed to the student in the closing narration.

media.title: Walkthrough of the 2×2 calendar trick for sum 36
media.context: Plays on M2.S4.T4.C40, a concept of its own that exists to carry this video. A rendered animation delivered from the manim video library.
media.description: A 100-second 2D whiteboard-style walkthrough of the 2×2 calendar trick on a clean white background. Frame 1 displays the August 2025 calendar with a 2×2 square highlighted. Frame 2 labels each of the four cells a, a+1, a+7, a+8 in turn. Frame 3 writes out the sum and simplifies it to 4a + 16. Frame 4 substitutes the given sum 36 to produce 4a + 16 = 36 and solves for a = 5. Frame 5 reveals the four dates 5, 6, 12, 13 inside the calendar. Text annotations only; no narration.
media.teaching_notes: Play AFTER the student has tried the calendar solver on their own 2×2 block. Pause at 60s, after 4a + 16 appears, and ask 'What equation ties this to the given sum 36?', this is the attempt-before-reveal moment. Pause near 85s, before the four dates are revealed, and ask 'Which four dates on the calendar match a = 5?' After Scene 5 ask 'Why do the offsets 0, 1, 7, 8 always sum to 16 no matter where the 2×2 sits on the calendar?' to stress the structural reason.
media.generation_prompt: Duration: 100 seconds. Style: 2D animation, clean whiteboard-style, step-by-step reveal on a pure white background with a handwritten-style calendar. Scene 1 (0, 20s): Problem statement, the August 2025 calendar is drawn; a 2×2 block is highlighted in Orange on an arbitrary location; a caption reads 'sum of the four dates = 36'. Scene 2 (20, 40s): Labels, the top-left cell is labelled a in Navy Blue; the top-right fills with a + 1; the bottom-left with a + 7; the bottom-right with a + 8; each +1, +7, +8 appears in Orange. Scene 3 (40, 60s): Sum setup, the four labels are stacked and added term by term; the a's collect into 4a and the constants 0 + 1 + 7 + 8 collect into 16; the line 4a + 16 appears in Navy Blue with 16 boxed in red. Pause at 60s: on-screen text asks 'What equation would you now write to find a?' Scene 4 (60, 85s): Solve, the line 4a + 16 = 36 appears; subtract 16 from both sides in Orange to get 4a = 20; divide both sides by 2 to get a = 5. Scene 5 (85, 100s): Reveal, a = 5 is substituted back; the four dates 5, 6, 12, 13 light up inside the calendar in red. Visual elements: Navy Blue for the fixed calendar layout and a, Orange for each +k offset and for the operations, red box around the combined constant 16 and the final four dates. Music: none; text-only annotations.

topics.summary: Four calendar dates are all built from one unknown, so their sum recovers them. Shape grids fall the same way, one single-unknown row at a time.

content.text: Pick a 2 by 2 block on a calendar. The top-left date is a. The date beside it is a plus 1, because dates rise by 1 along a row. The date below the top-left is a plus 7, because a week has 7 days, so dropping a row adds 7. The last date is a plus 8. Adding all four gives a plus (a plus 1) plus (a plus 7) plus (a plus 8), which is 4a plus 16. The key point is that all four cells share the same a, so the sum is one equation in one unknown. Given only the sum, you solve 4a plus 16 equals the sum for a, then rebuild every date. The plus 7 down-shift is what makes four dates behave like one unknown.

content.text: In a shape grid, each picture stands for a hidden number, and the last cell of a row is the sum of the shapes to its left. To crack it, look for a row that uses only one kind of shape, like star plus star equals 18. That row has a single unknown, so you can solve it: each star is 9. Now carry that value into a row that mixes shapes, such as star plus moon equals 15, which becomes 9 plus moon equals 15, so the moon is 6. The order matters. A row with two different unknown shapes cannot be solved on its own, so you always begin with a single-shape row and unlock the rest one step at a time.

topics.original_chunk: Pick a 2 by 2 block on a calendar. The top-left date is a. The date beside it is a plus 1, because dates rise by 1 along a row. The date below the top-left is a plus 7, because a week has 7 days, so dropping a row adds 7. The last date is a plus 8. Adding all four gives a plus (a plus 1) plus (a plus 7) plus (a plus 8), which is 4a plus 16. The key point is that all four cells share the same a, so the sum is one equation in one unknown. Given only the sum, you solve 4a plus 16 equals the sum for a, then rebuild every date. The plus 7 down-shift is what makes four dates behave like one unknown. learning_objectives.objective_text: Students will be able to infer why the four dates of a two by two calendar block behave like one hidden value, and determine that writing them as a, a plus 1, a plus 7, and a plus 8 makes their total 4a plus 16. They will explain that dropping a row adds 7 and every cell shares the same a, so solving 4a plus 16 equals the given sum recovers a and then rebuilds all four dates.
Examine the worked examples of recovering a calendar block from its sum, across different cases.
Examine the practised examples and practice questions involving recovering a calendar block from its sum, across different cases.

Students will be able to infer how a grid of shapes standing for hidden numbers can be untangled, and determine that a row using only one kind of shape fixes that shape's value at once. They will explain that carrying the found value into a row mixing two shapes leaves a single hidden value to solve, so a two-shape row can never be cracked on its own and the single-shape row must always be solved first.

media.title: Where does the biggest digit belong
media.context: This hook opens the topic on arranging digits for the largest product. Students can simplify expressions. The film must not name the winning arrangement and must not explain why the tempting one loses.
media.description: Take three different digits and build a two digit number times a one digit number. There are six ways to arrange them and they give wildly different products, and the tempting choice of the largest two digit number surprisingly loses.
media.teaching_notes: Learning objective: Arrange digits to give the largest or smallest product, and justify the choice. Key teaching points: 1) Each digit contributes according to the place it occupies. 2) The one digit multiplier reaches every part of the other number. 3) The greatest digit therefore does most work as the multiplier. 4) The same reasoning reversed gives the smallest product. Common misconceptions: 1) Students often build the largest two digit number without checking. 2) Students often assume the largest digit belongs in the tens place. Pause points: 0:22, at the end of and the tempting one loses: ask which arrangement the class expects to win. 0:22, just before the open question: ask what the multiplier actually multiplies. Questions to ask: before viewing, ask what thirty two times nine comes to. After viewing, ask where the biggest digit should go.

media.description: A 90-second 2D whiteboard-style walkthrough comparing 32×5 and 52×3 on a clean white background. Frame 1 shows both products side by side. Frame 2 expands 32×5 into 30×5 + 2×5 = 150 + 10 = 160. Frame 3 expands 52×3 into 50×3 + 2×3 = 150 + 6 = 156. Frame 4 marks the 150 as the shared part in both expansions and reduces the comparison to 10 versus 6. Frame 5 displays a caption noting that the larger contribution comes from pairing the largest digit with the largest place. Text annotations only; no narration.

Pause at 80s, before the rule appears, and ask 'What general rule can you state about which digit should be the multiplier?' Close by asking 'Would the same rule work if the two-digit number were bigger, say 62×5 versus 52×6?' to transfer the idea.

topics.summary: Among the six ways to place three digits, the greatest digit as the multiplier gives the largest product and the least digit as the multiplier gives the smallest, as place value explains.

content.text: Given three different digits to place as a two-digit number times a one-digit number, there are six arrangements. It is tempting to build the biggest two-digit number, like 93 times 2, but that wastes the large digit. The largest product instead puts the greatest digit as the single multiplier, because the multiplier multiplies the whole two-digit number, boosting both its tens and its ones. The other two digits form the two-digit number in decreasing order. So from 2, 3, 9 the winner is 32 times 9, which is 288, not 93 times 2, which is 186. Expanding two close rivals by place value shows their leading parts tie and the ones term decides, which is why the greatest digit belongs in the multiplier spot.

content.text: The smallest product works as a mirror of the largest. To make the product as small as possible, put the least digit as the single multiplier, because the multiplier acts on the whole two-digit number, so a small multiplier keeps every part of the product small. The other two digits form the two-digit number in increasing order. It is tempting to build the smallest two-digit number, like 46 times 7, but that leaves a large multiplier and pushes the product up. From 4, 6, 7 the smallest is 67 times 4, which is 268, not 46 times 7, which is 322. Expanding by place value shows that shrinking the multiplier shrinks both the tens and the ones part of the product.

topics.summary: Reversing the digits swaps the tens and ones, so subtracting leaves 9 times the digit difference and adding leaves 11 times the digit sum. Neither trick can fail.

content.text: Pick a two-digit number, reverse its digits, and subtract the smaller from the larger. The result is always a multiple of 9. Here is why. Write the number as 10a plus b, where a is the tens digit and b is the ones digit. Its reversal is 10b plus a. Subtracting gives 10a plus b minus 10b minus a, which tidies up to 9a minus 9b, that is 9 times (a minus b). Since a minus b is a whole number, the difference is nine copies of it, so dividing by 9 leaves no remainder and the quotient is exactly the difference of the two digits. The tens and ones digits swapping roles is what forces the 9, so the trick can never fail.

content.text: Now reverse a two-digit number and add it to the original. The total is always a multiple of 11. Write the number as 10a plus b and its reversal as 10b plus a. Adding gives 10a plus b plus 10b plus a, which is 11a plus 11b, that is 11 times (a plus b). So the sum is eleven copies of the digit sum, and dividing by 11 leaves no remainder while the quotient is exactly the sum of the two digits. This is a different trick from reversing and subtracting, which gives multiples of 9. Adding brings the tens and ones together as 11 times the digit sum, so a total like 88 is 11 times 8, not a multiple of 9. The place value forces it, so it never fails.

media.context: This is the chapter summary and it plays after the final topic. Every claim it makes has already been taught and practised, so nothing new appears and no fresh trick is designed. Its job is to make naming the unknown the thing that is remembered.
media.description: The film gathers the chapter together. Call the starting number a letter and every step of a trick becomes a line you can read, and the letter cancels itself out, which is why the finish is the same for everybody.
media.teaching_notes: Learning objective: Restate how naming the unknown explains every trick in the chapter. Key teaching points: 1) Naming the unknown turns steps into an expression. 2) A cancelling letter forces the same finish for everybody. 3) The pyramid top is a fixed combination of the bottom row. 4) Digit arrangement is settled by where the multiplier acts. 5) Place value algebra explains the reversal tricks. Common misconceptions: 1) Students often remember the outcomes rather than the method. 2) Students often think each trick needs its own explanation. Pause points: 0:30, at the end of the letter cancels: ask what happens to the letter by the end of a trick. 1:15, just before just a calculation: ask which of the four cards they would explain first. Questions to ask: before viewing, ask how they would design a trick landing on nine. After viewing, ask why the middle pyramid entry counts twice.

Frame 2 assembles the equation 60x − 10x − 5000 = 2000 step by step, with the price per dosa, the cost per dosa and the fixed cost appearing in turn. Frame 3 combines like terms to 50x − 5000 = 2000, then to 50x = 7000, and finally to x = 140. Frame 4 changes the selling price to ₹50; the equation becomes 40x − 5000 = 2000 and x = 175. Frame 5 displays a comparison chart showing how the dosa count varies with selling price. Text annotations only; no narration.
media.teaching_notes: Play AFTER the student has tried the equation builder at ₹60. Pause at 65s, after x = 140 is boxed, and ask 'Rewrite the equation when the selling price is ₹50, which coefficient changes?', this is the attempt-before-reveal moment. Pause near 85s, before the comparison chart, and ask 'Will the dosa count go up or down if the price drops from ₹60 to ₹50? Why?' Close by asking 'What selling price would make x = 100 for the same target profit? Set up the equation.' to transfer to a new case.
media.generation_prompt: Duration: 100 seconds. Style: 2D animation, clean whiteboard-style, step-by-step reveal on a pure white background with a small illustrated school-mela dosa cart in the corner. Scene 1 (0, 20s): Scene and setup, a caption describes the dosa cart selling each dosa for ₹60, with material cost ₹10 per dosa and a fixed stall cost of ₹5000 and a target profit of ₹2000; x stands for the number of dosas sold, written in Navy Blue. Scene 2 (20, 45s): Build the equation, 60x writes itself for revenue; ‒10x appears in Orange for material cost; ‒5000 appears in Orange for the fixed cost; the target 2000 goes on the right; the full line 60x − 10x − 5000 = 2000 is shown. Scene 3 (45, 65s): Solve, the 60x and 10x combine to 50x in red; subtracting ‒5000 moves to the right as +5000, giving 50x = 7000; dividing both sides by 50 gives x = 140 in Navy Blue, boxed in red. Pause at 65s: on-screen text asks 'What if the selling price were ₹50 instead? Rewrite the equation.' Scene 4 (65, 85s): New price, 60x is replaced by 50x; the combined term becomes 40x in Orange; the line 40x − 5000 = 2000 is solved to x = 175. Scene 5 (85, 100s): Comparison, a small chart shows 'price ₹60 → 140 dosas' and 'price ₹50 → 175 dosas' in two rows; a caption notes that lowering the price raises the dosa count. Visual elements: Navy Blue for x and the final answer, Orange for each cost term and for the rearrangement steps, red for the combined coefficient and the boxed answer. Music: none; text-only annotations.
media.instructions_for_student: Watch the animation on Walkthrough of the dosa-cart equation at two selling prices, then be ready to explain it in your own words.

subject: Mathematics
textbook: Mathematics, Textbook for Class 8 (NCERT)

objectives.objective_text: Students will be able to infer what a single letter records when a trick says think of a number, and determine that each instruction acting on the hidden number becomes an expression such as n plus 8, 3n, or 2n plus 4. They will explain that the result stays undetermined and shifts as the starting number shifts while the letter remains, and settles into one fixed value only once an actual number replaces the letter.
Examine the worked examples of a letter for a hidden number, across different cases.
Examine the practised examples and practice questions involving a letter for a hidden number, across different cases.

Students will be able to infer why a think of a number trick always announces the same ending, and determine that carrying the start as x through each step leaves x plus a fixed number before the final move. They will explain that subtracting the original number cancels the x and leaves only that fixed number, so every possible starting value lands on the identical answer and the outcome is forced rather than lucky.
Examine the worked examples of why the answer is always the same, across different cases.
Examine the practised examples and practice questions involving why the answer is always the same, across different cases.

Students will be able to infer why a single reported number can reveal a secret date, and determine that writing the month as M and the day as D drives the fixed steps to the form 100M plus 165 plus D. They will explain that subtracting 165 leaves 100M plus D, so the last two digits give the day and the hundreds give the month, letting any date be rebuilt from the final number alone.
Examine the worked examples of finding a hidden date from one number, across different cases.
Examine the practised examples and practice questions involving finding a hidden date from one number, across different cases.

Students will be able to infer how a whole number pyramid grows from its bottom row, and determine that every brick equals the sum of the two bricks directly below it, so a three-row base yields two middle bricks and one top brick. They will explain that nothing above needs to be given because the rule pushes values upward, and that a middle bottom brick feeds two sums, so a small change low down can spread far up.

Students will be able to infer how a pyramid with a blank bottom can still be completed, and determine that naming a blank bottom brick with a letter turns a given brick above into one equation in that letter. They will explain that solving it pins the missing value, and that the blank brick appears twice as a 2c term because it feeds both middle bricks, so subtracting it only once gives the wrong answer.
Examine the worked examples of working a pyramid backward, across different cases.
Examine the practised examples and practice questions involving working a pyramid backward, across different cases.

Students will be able to infer why the top of a three-row pyramid is not the plain total of its bottom row, and determine that writing the base as a, b, c makes the top equal a plus 2b plus c. They will explain that the middle brick b sits under both middle bricks and so is doubled while the corners a and c count once, and that a four-row base shifts the weights to 1, 3, 3, 1.
Examine the worked examples of the top as a plus 2b plus c, across different cases.
Examine the practised examples and practice questions involving the top as a plus 2b plus c, across different cases.

Students will be able to infer why the four dates of a two by two calendar block behave like one hidden value, and determine that writing them as a, a plus 1, a plus 7, and a plus 8 makes their total 4a plus 16. They will explain that dropping a row adds 7 and every cell shares the same a, so solving 4a plus 16 equals the given sum recovers a and then rebuilds all four dates.
Examine the worked examples of recovering a calendar block from its sum, across different cases.
Examine the practised examples and practice questions involving recovering a calendar block from its sum, across different cases.

Students will be able to infer how a grid of shapes standing for hidden numbers can be untangled, and determine that a row using only one kind of shape fixes that shape's value at once. They will explain that carrying the found value into a row mixing two shapes leaves a single hidden value to solve, so a two-shape row can never be cracked on its own and the single-shape row must always be solved first.

Students will be able to infer which arrangement of three digits gives the largest two-digit by one-digit product, and determine that placing the greatest digit as the single multiplier, with the other two forming the two-digit number in decreasing order, wins rather than building the biggest two-digit number. They will explain that the multiplier acts on the whole two-digit number, and expanding two close rivals by place value shows their leading parts tie while the ones term decides.

Students will be able to infer which arrangement of three digits gives the smallest two-digit by one-digit product, and determine that placing the least digit as the single multiplier, with the other two forming the two-digit number in increasing order, beats building the smallest two-digit number. They will explain that a small multiplier keeps every part of the product small, mirroring the largest-product rule, so shrinking the multiplier shrinks both the tens and the ones part.

Students will be able to infer why reversing a two-digit number and subtracting always yields a multiple of 9, and determine that writing the number as 10a plus b and its reversal as 10b plus a makes the difference 9 times a minus b. They will explain that a minus b is a whole number, so the result is nine copies of it and dividing by 9 leaves no remainder, so no two-digit number can break the rule.

Students will be able to infer why reversing a two-digit number and adding always yields a multiple of 11, and determine that writing the number as 10a plus b and its reversal as 10b plus a makes the sum 11 times a plus b. They will explain that the total is eleven copies of the digit sum so dividing by 11 leaves no remainder, and that this differs from reversing and subtracting, which forces a multiple of 9.

how_to_use.intro: This chapter turns number tricks and puzzles into algebra. Each section pairs a short, plain explanation with one interactive tool, so the trick is run and puzzled over before its reason is revealed.

points.text: Every idea starts as a puzzle on the tool, and the surprise comes before the explanation.
points.title: Run the trick first

points.text: The punchline of every section is the same move: swap the mystery number for a letter and the reason the trick works appears.
points.title: Replace the number with a letter

points.text: Worked examples are demonstrated in Learn mode, then the same skill is practised in Play mode where answers turn green or red.
points.title: Learn then Play

points.text: After the tool-answered practice, four reasoning items ask the learner to apply, work backwards, explain, and catch a deliberate mistake.
points.title: Think it through

points.text: Even on reasoning items the tool remains on screen as an aid; tool_needed only describes how the answer is entered.
points.title: The tool stays visible

how_to_use.heading: How to use this chapter

summary_stats.counts_note: One distinct tool per concept; each tool runs four mods (AI demo, Learn, Practice, Free Play), with one objective each for AI demo, Learn and Practice and none for Free Play.
summary_stats.videos_note: One 30 to 40 second curiosity hook video per topic, plus a chapter intro video and a chapter summary video of 1 to 2 minutes each.
summary_stats.tool_needed_note: Per-item boolean for how the ANSWER is entered, NOT whether to show the tool. The frontend ALWAYS renders the tool. true = the answer must be produced through the tool. false = the student reasons it out (typed/spoken) and the tool stays on screen as an aid.
summary_stats.solved_examples_note: Each solved example carries a first-person 'reasoning' field that generalises the method.
summary_stats.practice_problems_note: 172 practice items in all = (12 microconcepts x 10 tool-answered) + (12 x 4 reasoning items) + 4 proof items on the concepts that state a general claim.
summary_stats.question_repository_note: Worked-example and practice questions are no longer inline. Each learn/practice concept carries a question_bank_ref into question_repository.json; the teacher agent pulls questions from the repository at teach time. The teaching (AI-demo) concept keeps its inline source_ai_reasoning block.

authoring_rules.nesting: Each objective contains exactly one concept; each concept contains its solved examples then its practice questions.
authoring_rules.solved_examples: At least 10 per microconcept; each is demonstrated on that section's tool with numbered steps, a final answer and first-person reasoning that models how to think, not just which buttons to press.
authoring_rules.practice_questions: At least 10 tool-answered items per microconcept (marked right/wrong on the tool), followed by exactly 4 reasoning items: application, reverse, explain, error_spotting. A concept that states a general claim carries a 5th reasoning item, proof, between explain and error_spotting.

mods.does: The AI teaches the whole concept and works the higher-order reasoning questions (application, reverse, explain, error-spotting) with full step-by-step explanations, with the tool on screen; the student only watches.
The AI demonstrates the worked examples one step at a time on the tool.
The student answers the tool-answered practice questions that reinforce the worked examples.
The student freely solves any question of the same kind on the tool, neither taught nor scored.

tool_mods_legend.note: Every tool runs four mods. Teach mods are AI operated; practice and play are student operated.
